A second finding sharpens the scope problem: the median gap between initial access and handoff to a second threat group collapsed from over 8 hours in 2022 to 22 seconds by 2025. You are often reconstructing two separate intrusion sets with different tooling and different goals, and the quiet one came first.

- Exfiltration is confirmed until you prove otherwise. CISA's November 2025 Akira advisory (co-authored with the FBI, Europol EC3, and partners in France 🇫🇷, Germany 🇩🇪, and the Netherlands 🇳🇱) records cases where Akira operators exfiltrated data within two hours of initial access, and puts claimed proceeds at roughly $244.17 million as of late September 2025. The tooling is ordinary: FileZilla and WinRAR for staging, WinSCP and RClone for transfer, Mega for cloud storage, Ngrok for tunneling. Hunt on outbound volume and destination, not malware signatures. A single host pushing tens of gigabytes to a consumer cloud endpoint over a weekend is your signal.

- Backup integrity gates everything downstream. M-Trends 2026 describes a deliberate shift toward recovery denial, with groups including those using REDBIKE and AGENDA actively targeting backup infrastructure, identity services, and virtualization management planes, including deleting backup objects from cloud storage. The Akira advisory documents the simpler version: volume shadow copies removed with a short PowerShell command. Before quoting any recovery time, restore one real file, confirm immutability or object lock is active today, and verify whether the backup server authenticates against the same domain you are about to rebuild. An untested backup is a hope, not a measurement.

- Identity is where the root cause investigation lives. The Akira advisory documents credential dumping via Mimikatz and LaZagne, LSASS memory access, and Kerberoasting against service accounts. Any of those means the credentials you are resetting were readable long before encryption started. Key questions to answer before any rebuild: which account moved first, was MFA absent or bypassed, which systems did that account touch in the 30 days prior, and do your domain controllers still hold logs covering that window. Recovery sequencing matters too: a clean domain controller in an isolated segment comes first, then data restoration into that clean environment. Restoring a compromised system in place preserves whatever persistence the access broker installed.

- Most first days fail on authority, not technique. The runbook covers isolation and forensics. It names nobody. The ransom question, the decision to take a production line offline, and the notification clock for insurers and regulators all land simultaneously on whoever happens to be in the room, and they run at different speeds on different trigger events.

Practitioner takeaway: This week, do one of three things. Restore a file from your newest backup and time it. Write three decision-makers and three deputies into your IR plan's authority section. Audit every remote access path for MFA enforcement. The Akira advisory IOC list, including the named transfer tools and VPN access vector detail, is in the report. Run your next tabletop on a Friday at 17:00 with the people who would actually take the call.

item.title: Antino Backdoor Uses Outlook and OneDrive for C2 in China-Nexus Espionage Campaign
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 -nexus UAT-11587 deploys Antino, a Rust backdoor that hides C2 entirely inside Microsoft 365, routing commands through Outlook and OneDrive to blend into legitimate cloud traffic across eight Asian governments.
Key findings:
- Antino (slc.dll) is a Rust-compiled Windows backdoor loaded via DLL sideloading using the legitimate Microsoft-signed binary GatherOsState.exe. Once active, it polls the threat actor's Outlook mailbox every 10 seconds for messages with the subject prefix "command_req_[session_id]" and uses OneDrive for heartbeat and file transfer. There is no dedicated C2 server to block or alert on. The Microsoft Graph API is the only outbound channel.
- The five-stage delivery chain starts with a spear-phishing email carrying a fake Gmail attachment preview widget, built from four Base64-encoded inline PNG images and an anchor tag pointing to a Cloudflare Pages URL. That URL delivers an HTA or WSF stager, which retrieves a JavaScript downloader, which triggers a .NET deserialization chain loading TestAssembly.dll, which finally drops and launches Antino. A decoy Calculator binary and a lure document open simultaneously to mask the install.
- Two forensic breadcrumbs tie the builds to mainland China 🇨🇳: nearly a dozen Antino Cargo registry paths reference rsproxy[.]cn, a domestic Rust mirror for mainland developers, and an associated JavaScript downloader references d32tpl7xt7175h.cloudfront[.]net, a CloudFront domain previously linked to Chinese-affiliated UNC6384. Lure documents carry zh-CN language metadata and Simplified Chinese 🇨🇳 authorship, and phishing headers show UTC+08:00.
- Antino abuses the Windows Scripted Diagnostics framework to run attacker-controlled PowerShell through legitimate Windows components, deliberately breaking the behavioral link between the implant and the PowerShell activity. Talos notes this complicates attribution but does not eliminate observable PowerShell, file-creation, or Registry telemetry on the host.
- UAT-11587 has targeted 16 entities across Taiwan 🇹🇼, India 🇮🇳, the Philippines 🇵🇭, Cambodia 🇰🇭, Pakistan 🇵🇰, Thailand 🇹🇭, Myanmar 🇲🇲, and Syria, with a concentrated wave on June 8 and 9, 2026 hitting dozens of government IT systems. The group shares some overlap with Jewelbug and clusters including CL-STA-0049, Earth Alux, Ink Dragon, and REF7707, though Cisco Talos tracks UAT-11587 as a separate activity set.
Practitioner takeaway: Because all C2 rides Microsoft Graph, perimeter blocks and suspicious-IP detections will miss this entirely. Hunt instead on the host: look for GatherOsState.exe loading an unexpected DLL (slc.dll), PowerShell or cmd.exe spawned under the Windows Scripted Diagnostics framework (sdiagnhost.exe lineage), and Microsoft Graph OAuth token requests issued by non-browser, non-Office processes. In mail logs, search for Outlook folder polling patterns with the subject prefix "command_req_" against accounts that do not belong to recognized mail clients. File-creation and Registry telemetry around the Antino install remain observable per Talos. Full IOC list and detection content are in the Cisco Talos report.

item.title: Lunex Uses BYOVD to Disable Security Monitoring and Deploy Persistent Stealer
item.description:
LunexStealer uses PDB-guided BYOVD via a vulnerable AMD driver (CVE-2023-20598) to silently blind endpoint security before stealing credentials and planting a persistent Native Messaging Host on Ukrainian 🇺🇦 targets.
Key findings:
- The infection chain starts with a fake CAPTCHA page on uasputnik[.]com, which instructs victims to run an msiexec command that silently installs a malicious MSI from %LOCALAPPDATA%, no admin required at first. LunexLoader then fakes a trusted Windows binary via PEB manipulation, abuses the CMSTPLUA COM object for UAC bypass, and installs AMD's PDFWKRNL.sys (CVE-2023-20598) as a service, gaining kernel read/write through exposed IOCTL calls, all before the stealer touches disk.
- The BYOVD implementation is unusually surgical. LunexLoader reads the victim's ntoskrnl.exe, extracts the PDB GUID for the running kernel build, and pulls matching symbols from Microsoft's Symbol Server using curl.exe. It then parses the PDB to resolve exact offsets for process, thread, and image-load callback tables, making the technique version-agnostic across Windows 10 and 11. It zeros callback entries belonging to a 20-entry blocklist that includes Microsoft Defender, CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, ESET, Elastic, Kaspersky, Dr[.]Web, Sysmon, and Windows Filter Manager. Targeting Filter Manager can disable entire classes of minifilter-based products at once. Validated testing found that neither HVCI nor the then-current Microsoft Vulnerable Driver Blocklist blocked the specific PDFWKRNL.sys variant used.
- LunexStealer targets Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Brave, Yandex Browser, Opera, Opera GX, and Vivaldi, pulling credentials, cookies, tokens, and card data. It handles Chrome App-Bound Encryption and ChaCha20-Poly1305 (versions 10, 11, and 20). Crypto wallet targets include Bitcoin Core, Litecoin, Exodus, Atomic Wallet, Electrum, MetaMask, OKX Wallet, and SafePal Wallet.
- Persistence is layered: a registry Run key, a hidden scheduled task named psychedelicloveUtils, and Chrome and Edge Native Messaging Host registrations under the name com.lunex.explorer. The Native Messaging Host embeds PowerShell capable of drive enumeration, directory listing, file read/write, file download, and arbitrary execution. Ontinue confirmed it survives deletion of the stealer binary, reboots, and browser restarts, meaning removing LunexStealer.exe is not remediation.
- Ontinue identified 28 Lunex panels across 13 countries and assesses the platform as a Russian-speaking MaaS operation with CIS alignment, sold to independent criminal operators. The "Psychedelic" operator tag appears in the scheduled task name psychedelicloveUtils. Three samples are confirmed associated with this activity: bf14cd6c3328ebd08e940478b5d1da04e9e5aa576d045d41950bf4f1e2456dd8, 6e8b49cf70bf854e8c59c7d27cefa89406caf8978461190dabb86dafcd8554e1, and 06f434695f93d7fd11eeff71358ff69fed79d310a66d993bbcc4ff979c117c90.
Responder takeaway: Do not treat a live EDR process as proof of functioning visibility after a BYOVD incident. Hunt for curl.exe contacting Microsoft's Symbol Server, PDFWKRNL.sys loaded as a service, and the Native Messaging Host registry entries for com.lunex.explorer in both HKCU and HKLM Chrome and Edge NativeMessagingHosts keys. Check for a scheduled task named psychedelicloveUtils. On any system where LunexLoader ran, assume kernel callbacks may have been zeroed and validate telemetry coverage independently before trusting endpoint logs from that window.

item.title: Analyzing Windows BAM and DAM with Belkasoft X
item.description:
Windows BAM and DAM registry artifacts record executable paths, user SIDs, and execution timestamps, giving responders a direct answer to "what ran and who ran it" even after the binary is gone.
Key findings:
- BAM lives at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\bam\State\UserSettings\{SID} on Windows 10 1809 and later. Pre-1809 systems used \UserSettings without the \State\ prefix. Check both paths before concluding a user has no BAM data. Each value name is the executable path in NT device notation (e.g. \Device\HarddiskVolume3\Users\rsmith\Downloads\tool.exe) and the REG_BINARY data opens with an 8-byte little-endian Windows FILETIME. Do not assume the HarddiskVolume number maps to a specific drive letter without resolving the system's volume mappings. Packaged apps appear by Package Family Name, not a file path.
- Retention is short, roughly seven days by default, controlled by the UserSettingsLifetimeMs value under the BAM control key. If the SYSTEM hive lands on your bench two weeks after an alert, the record is likely already gone. Collect the hive early during triage, not as an afterthought.
- DAM follows the same registry structure and FILETIME format but is populated primarily on devices that support Modern Standby (tablets, lightweight laptops). An empty dam key on a desktop workstation is not evidence of deletion. Run powercfg /a on a live system to confirm whether Modern Standby is supported before commenting on an absent DAM.
- BAM does not capture everything. Console tools launched from an existing shell (cmd.exe, powershell.exe) do not get their own BAM entry, only the shell does. Applications run from network shares or removable media are generally not recorded. The artifact links execution to a SID, not to a person at the keyboard, and it records no command-line arguments, parent process, or exit code.
- These artifacts gain investigative weight through correlation. A BAM entry showing a suspicious executable path can be paired with a Prefetch file (C:\Windows\Prefetch) confirming execution count and load-time file references, UserAssist for GUI execution statistics, LNK files for file and folder access context, and Shellbags (USRCLASS.DAT, NTUSER.DAT) for folder browsing history. The combined timeline reconstructs behavior that no single artifact captures alone.
Practitioner takeaway: During triage, pull the SYSTEM hive immediately. To decode a BAM timestamp manually, take the first 8 bytes of the REG_BINARY value, reverse byte order to most-significant-byte-first, interpret as a 64-bit unsigned integer, and convert from Windows FILETIME (100-nanosecond intervals since 1601-01-01 UTC). For the example in the report, EB E6 4C 41 F0 86 DA 01 resolves to April 5, 2024, 00:29:00 UTC. When hunting for lateral tool transfer or malware staging, query BAM for executable paths under user Download or temp directories and cross-reference against Prefetch run counts. If a BAM entry exists but Prefetch has no corresponding file, treat that discrepancy as a lead worth pursuing.

For the example in the report, EB E6 4C 41 F0 86 DA 01 resolves to April 5, 2024, 00:29:00 UTC. When hunting for lateral tool transfer or malware staging, query BAM for executable paths under user Download or temp directories and cross-reference against Prefetch run counts. If a BAM entry exists but Prefetch has no corresponding file, treat that discrepancy as a lead worth pursuing.

item.title: Anatomy of an Attack - TerminalFix: When a Workstation Becomes a Network Pivot
item.description:
TerminalFix, a ClickFix variant linked to Vice Spider, turns a browsing workstation into a network pivot through DLL sideloading, steganographic payloads, and a WebSocket reverse tunnel, culminating in attempted ransomware and double extortion at German 🇩🇪 state institutions.
Key findings:
- The attack opens with a fake Cloudflare verification overlay served from compromised websites. Unlike standard ClickFix, which uses the Windows Run dialog, TerminalFix directs victims to paste multiline commands into PowerShell or Windows Terminal. PowerShell then pulls a ZIP archive to C:\ProgramData, where a batch script handles the next stage while the fake verification screen keeps the user distracted. Browser logs showing a suspicious verification page followed by concurrent PowerShell execution and a ZIP download are your earliest forensic signal.
- Phase 2 uses DLL sideloading: the ZIP delivers the legitimate Microsoft-signed LockScreenContentServer.exe alongside a malicious dui70.dll masquerading as "Windows DirectUI Engine." The executable loads the sideloaded DLL, giving the malicious code trusted-process cover. PowerShell then retrieves PNG files via HTTP POST from actor infrastructure, reconstructing binary payloads from pixel data using steganography. Hunt for LockScreenContentServer.exe loading dui70.dll from an unexpected path, and for PowerShell writing executables or DLLs to disk after HTTP POST requests for PNG files.
- Persistence lands on two mechanisms: a Registry Run key and an hourly scheduled task relaunching the payload independent of the browser session. AD reconnaissance follows immediately: nltest /domain_trusts, net group "domain admins" /domain, computer object queries, and server pings map domain relationships, privileged accounts, and reachable hosts. A workstation suddenly issuing these commands is an anomaly worth triaging fast.
- The C2 channel runs through pythonw.exe executing client[.]py, which connects to actor-controlled gitnow[.]dev:443 and upgrades to WebSocket over TLS at /tunnel. On September 22, 2026, gitnow[.]dev resolved to 92.118.126[.]201 hosted by BlueVPS OU. That host was found to contain shell history, Kerberos ticket caches, AD tooling including Certipy, Impacket, Krbrelayx, noPac, PetitPotam, PrintNightmare, and CertiGhost, plus CA enumeration outputs and relay logs. The operator attempted ntlmrelayx through ProxyChains against an internal certificate service to impersonate a domain controller. Two additional infrastructure domains registered August 12, 2026 on BlueVPS OU: bestsocialmedianewspapper[.]com at 45.66.249[.]112 and offlineupdater[.]com at 92.118.126[.]225.
- German 🇩🇪 incident reporting confirms real-world impact: BSI was notified of a state institution compromise matching the TerminalFix pattern in August, with actors attempting ransomware deployment and data exfiltration for double extortion. German 🇩🇪 media linked the campaign to Vice Spider. The infected workstation becomes a relay, meaning the risk extends to every internal system reachable from it while the tunnel was active.
Practitioner takeaway: Reconstruct the workstation's connection timeline around the window when pythonw.exe was running. Enumerate every internal destination it contacted while gitnow[.]dev was active, those are your lateral movement candidates. Pull Registry Run entries and scheduled tasks for payload relaunch commands, and check file servers for encryption or staging activity. The IOC list with the three actor domains and associated IPs is in the ExtraHop report.

item.title: AI agent exploits Zammad zero-days in DIVD breach: What we know and how to detect it
item.description:
An AI agent chained two Zammad zero-days to breach DIVD, reaching root in seconds and exfiltrating volunteer data, CSIRT ticket content, and potentially sensitive vulnerability research before defenders could respond.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-102489 (CVSS 8.7) is a low-complexity, no-privileges-required RCE affecting Zammad 6.3.0 to 6.5.4, exploitable over the public internet. CVE-2026-102490 (CVSS 8.5) is a local privilege escalation affecting all versions 1.5.0 to 7.1.0-alpha. Chained together, they score 9.4 critical. Both were zero-days at the time of exploitation, with no patch existing before the attack. Zammad 7.0.0 and later are not vulnerable to CVE-2026-102489 but remain exposed to the LPE until a fix is released.
- The agentic threat actor (ATA) is identifiable by behavioral signatures no human attacker leaves: self-documenting shell comments explaining each action ("no phishing," "no spam"), non-deterministic decisions chosen at machine speed after every step, and self-interference where its own password spraying disrupted a simultaneous MitM attempt. No human operator or group has claimed the attack as of publication.
- The attack chain ran: RCE as the zammad service user via CVE-2026-102489, immediate privilege escalation to root via CVE-2026-102490, credential harvesting from configuration files and stored API tokens, password spraying, and finally data exfiltration. DIVD confirmed volunteers' email addresses were taken, CSIRT ticket content including reported vulnerability details, masked credential dumps, and IP addresses of vulnerable systems were at minimum partially extracted, with Jira, Confluence, Slack, GitHub, GitLab, and sensitive research data still under investigation.
- Detection does not require knowing the CVE. The behaviors are high-fidelity and consistent regardless of exploit: the zammad user spawning an interactive shell, setuid-family syscalls from a service account, new root-owned child processes under the application tree, mass reads of credential and config files, and outbound connections to destinations the helpdesk segment has never contacted. Falco open-source rules covering these stages include Non sudo setuid, Set Setuid or Setgid bit, Change thread namespace, Potential Local Privilege Escalation via Environment Variables Misuse, and sudo potential privilege escalation.
- Network segmentation was the containment control that mattered. DIVD's segmentation stopped the agent from moving deeper, and a datacenter-wide access cut was required to halt the operation entirely. A default-deny egress policy on the helpdesk segment turns a quiet exfiltration into a blocked connection.
Practitioner takeaway: If you run Zammad, upgrade to 7.0.0 or later immediately or take the instance offline, then preserve /var/log/zammad and /var/log/nginx before rebuilding, and run DIVD's detection script against those logs. A clean log result does not equal a clean host since root access was achieved, so rotate every credential stored on or reachable from the host regardless. Hunt for unfamiliar processes, files in temp directories, and any outbound connection the helpdesk host has not made before. Pre-authorize automated containment for service-account shell-spawn and privilege-escalation alerts: an ATA that reaches root in seconds will not wait for a ticket. Full IOC list and DIVD's detection script are available at csirt.divd[.]nl/cases/DIVD-2026-00015/.

item.title: SMTP is the key: BPFDoor and AVERAT hitting the network edge
item.description:
BPFDoor, Rekoobe, and a new Linux implant called AVERAT are hitting telecom edge appliances and mail-security gateways across South Korea 🇰🇷 and Taiwan 🇹🇼, using SMTP port 25 as C2 camouflage and fileless staging to survive on embedded devices with no on-disk trace.
Key findings:
- The attack chain opens with a dropper (SHA-256: 2bedc26d4b29b435c21962beed7db21188a0219a0d28334bba8b4fb1656d7b15) that derives its AES-128-ECB key from SHA1("ShareTech"), pointing squarely at ShareTech appliances. It copies two binaries from /addpkg/sbin/ into /sbin as ntpdate and udevds, executes them, then unlinks both within ten seconds. Both processes keep running without an on-disk image: /proc/pid/exe resolves to "(deleted)" and grepping /sbin finds nothing. The dropper re-executes as a watchdog and relies on the firmware's own package startup to survive reboots, so there is no persistence code to find. Gate artifacts to hunt: /tmp/flag (precondition), /HDD/ms6x2xTo64/updIptable.php (shell script disguised as PHP), and /HDD/ms6x2xTo64/execProcEnd (watchdog marker).
- AVERAT (six builds, all recovered from /sbin/udevds) connects outbound on TCP/25, issues EHLO and STARTTLS, then runs its own hand-rolled TLS session authenticated with magic value 1571 (0x0623). Check-ins occur every 600-699 seconds and persist the interval to a hidden state file: /var/lib/.db, /var/lib/.sencha, /var/lib/.us, or /var/lib/.a depending on build. The 276-byte encrypted config blob (RC4, key derived from its own first 16 bytes) holds three C2 host/port slots. C2 infrastructure splits between attacker-registered domains (mx.zxopfds[.]com, spam.suwaccqi[.]com, mx1.wwstifsteel[.]com) and hardcoded consumer-broadband IPs (59.125.211[.]65, 122.116.138[.]33, 1.34.200[.]85) confirmed as compromised Chunghwa Telecom HiNet (AS3462) CPE: a fuel retailer's Synology NAS, an end-of-life NetKlass SMB appliance, and a Dahua DH-XVR5116HS-I3 CCTV recorder. All three also run operator-installed PPTP on 1723 with a byte-identical banner, making each node a dual-purpose relay and VPN foothold. Command code 1618 opens a proxy or port-forward through the compromised appliance; the reboot handler (code 916) calls sync() before forcing a kernel restart, deliberately flushing volatile state while leaving disk persistence intact.
- The South Korean 🇰🇷 BPFDoor cluster (SHA-256: a37ea9897221d4495b538de72b74f2aa1d2ff09b7b6dcedd395aee58931adbf3 and 7e667ba5f9df912e02275d3cfe3809d16f822fe776f4035c84b118ebd925b1b5) uses magic bytes 0x6693 (UDP), 0x4274 (TCP), and 0x7820 (ICMP), passwords gZbpx0 (reverse shell) and sT21xf (bind shell), and impersonates /var/run/spamsniper.pid, directly naming SpamSniper anti-spam software as the masquerade target. The data-plane BPFDoor pair (a6f3b7f932761fb1fd5e74123f2482e36c65dd13e769af2ce08c65da195bfa7a and 4435fcd6862921092614dbeaa880e4192352984686ebcd98f0ba13ee8e226ef9) spoofs ora_ppmond and /sniper/snipe/bin/dtnpd respectively, integrating Tiny Shell with single-byte S/U/D commands for shell, upload, and download. The BPF Rekoobe sample (652508a9cf40bee883dc0e5e219dfeba71fe7dac591d01c89f74c21f73b4963f) sniffs for traffic where src port and dst port both equal 25, authenticated with a 32-byte magic sequence and XOR key uvTIgh47,[@]R, then spoofs /sniper/autorun/rblsmtpd to blend with a mail gateway's expected process list. On a SpamSniper appliance, a packet with src=25 dst=25 matches the legitimate MTA relay firewall rule and reaches the raw socket before stateful inspection.
- The updated BPFDoor controller now supports HTTPS POST tunneling (-g flag, dogetlogin function) to defeat static network signatures: it sends mathematically padded requests (e.g., POST /admin/login.aspx?id=99990) so the string "9999" lands at exactly offset 26 of the TCP payload as a dynamic reference point. The controller spoofs /usr/sbin/abrtd via PR_SET_NAME. New flags include -H for a hidden relay IP, -D to customize URI paths for log blending, and -v for debug output. MITRE ATT&CK techniques documented across both clusters include T1205.002 (Socket Filters), T1036.004/T1036.005 (Masquerading), T1070.003 (Clear Command History), T1071.003 (Mail Protocols), T1573.001 (Symmetric Cryptography), T1090 (Proxy), and T1584.008 (Compromise Infrastructure: Network Devices), among others in the report.
Takeaway for responders: File-based detection on these appliances will fail because nothing survives in /sbin. Hunt for Linux processes where /proc/pid/exe shows "(deleted)", inspect memory maps for executable pages with no backing file, and alert on the process-tree sequence of sh -c against a .php path followed by cp and chmod into /sbin then rm -rf of the same path within ten seconds. On the network, flag outbound TCP/25 from processes that are not mail services, especially where the destination resolves to consumer-grade CPE. Check for PPTP on 1723 on edge appliances that have no business running it. Full IOC tables, cryptographic constants, host artifacts, and YARA rules are available in the Rapid7 report and in Rapid7's Intelligence Hub.

item.title: The NetScaler Zero-Day Siege and Pre-Auth RCE Chains : Technical Analysis and Exposure Assessment
item.description:
ShinyHunters claims FBIJobs[.]gov breach via Oracle PeopleSoft RCE. CVE-2026-35273 (CVSS 9.8) WAF bypass is the leading initial access hypothesis, with web shells and SIDEEYE backdoor confirmed in the wider campaign.
Key details:
- CVE-2026-35273 is a critical unauthenticated RCE in Oracle PeopleSoft's Environment Management Hub (PSEMHUB), triggered via Java deserialization. ShinyHunters exploited it as a zero-day May 27 to June 9, 2026 against 100+ organizations before Oracle's June 10 out-of-band patch. The renewed September 2026 wave uses /%50SEMHUB/ as the request path: %50 is URL-encoded "P", which WebLogic decodes and routes normally while WAF rules matching the literal string /PSEMHUB/ pass it clean. Organizations that blocked the path but never patched are re-exposed. Hunt PIA WebLogic access logs for that encoded path and for bursts of 5 to 15 POST requests to /hub from external IPs, a pattern researchers observed used to confirm exploitability.
- Post-exploitation toolset documented in the September 25 Mandiant report: x.jsp (command execution web shell), u.jsp (chunked file upload stager, SHA-256 2bee941fb40519d0d1ec52bd79a8f63fc65aac6455c8f2d6b668e3360dfdb5d7), Ple64.exe SIDEEYE loader (SHA-256 3ba215692665513abfffd4e815c5c45f2d41e5dcc4283a2a3b740930c5c417c3), Neo-reGeorg tunnel.jsp and tunnel.jspx for SOCKS proxying, and MeshAgent for persistent remote access via winmanage-me[.]network and azurenetfiles[.]net. A fileless execution variant leaves no JSP on disk, so JSP-based detections alone are not sufficient.
- The confirmed infrastructure includes attack controller 5.199.162[.]157, exfiltration staging host 104.219.234[.]138, SIDEEYE C2 at 162.219.30[.]165 over TCP 3333/3334, staging range 142.11.200[.]186 to 142.11.200[.]190 (May to June 2026), and MeshAgent enrollment domain enroll.azuredevice[.]cloud. X.jsp and the Neo-reGeorg tunnel hashes vary per victim: hunt by file name and path in PSEMHUB.war and PORTAL.war, not by hash alone.
- The FBIJobs[.]gov intrusion claimed by ShinyHunters involves an alleged 2 to 3 TB exfiltration including names, home addresses, spouse details, Social Security numbers, unit assignments, and psychiatric and medical files. A 5,000-record sample was judged authentic by 404 Media and Reuters. An internal FBI memo reported by The New York Times states the Bureau is operating under the assumption that personal data of all FBI employees was exfiltrated. The FBI has not confirmed the entry point, scope, or which systems were accessed. If the MedLink, Criminal Justice, BEAST, and AWS GovCloud claims hold, this is a segmentation failure: a public recruitment portal reaching medical and investigative systems.

item.title: CVE-2026-104286: FortiMail Path Traversal Vulnerability Actively Exploited
item.description:
CVE-2026-104286 is a zero-day path traversal in FortiMail actively exploited in the wild with no patch available. Unauthenticated attackers are writing files outside intended directories to achieve remote code execution and full mail gateway compromise.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-104286 affects FortiMail 7.2 through 8.0.1 across all current release lines. Exploitation is unauthenticated: a crafted request abuses the IBE feature to write arbitrary files outside the intended directory, which attackers are leveraging to drop malicious binaries and a modified ld[.]so.preload for persistent, system-wide code injection on every process launch. No patch exists. Fortinet's current guidance is to disable the IBE feature via CLI (config system encryption ibe / set status disable / end) or restrict management interface access to trusted private networks only.
- Post-exploitation forensic artifacts are well-defined. Look for the following added or modified files on disk: /data/lib/liblog.so (SHA256: 8015f34dc84922b03688399d7f9fe7a00361789f7e420c7e2a2cdb23e75cef84), /data/bin/webconsole (SHA256: 7a6cea9f5c9e2e9994d4e3c4da73f86cf5acd05ea5d312c066c9d1dafd69ee38), /data/bin/mailservice (SHA256: 4000276a150a165d3c2537d1e19fb393c4de8333076a16655e28059cae82157b), a modified /bin/smit (SHA256: 77324ac428bde86d351fc5fc06f6d64a6bfe737dfb2743df1d4c5ac2418a5b6a), and critically /data/etc/ld.so.preload (SHA256: 8953ec7960b09f544a880b072ad4e6cfda7a8303f486251d3478dcfdfbac23b6). A modified /data/migadmin.tar.gz and /data/etc/httpd.conf round out the tampered file set.
- The attacker established data exfiltration via a rogue archive account. Log evidence shows an "archive234" account added through CLI with rotation to a remote IP at 79.141.169[.]187 via the config system archive path, rotating stored mail to /uploads. A second IP, 45.129.0[.]192, appears in the IOC set. The cron-triggered shell command visible in logs (type=event subtype=system pri=debug user=system ui=cron msg="(root) CMD (/bin/sh -c 'O=/migadmin...") shows persistence operating through scheduled execution. The admin logout from a null UI session and the IBE BufferException log entries are early indicators of exploitation attempts worth hunting in FortiMail event logs.
- Scope and impact are significant. FortiMail sits at the boundary of email infrastructure, storing messages, credentials, and maintaining trusted connections to internal mail systems. Full compromise gives an attacker access to email content, potential credential harvesting from stored mail, and a pivot point into connected environments.
Takeaway: Pull FortiMail logs immediately and grep for the cron CMD pattern referencing /migadmin, archive account additions with remote-ip fields pointing outside your environment, and admin logout events from null UI sessions. Hash-check the six files listed above against your FortiMail filesystem. Block 79.141.169[.]187 and 45.129.0[.]192 at the perimeter. Apply the IBE disable workaround now. Full IOC list including file hashes and IPs is in the Truesec report.

item.title: Pwn2Own Ireland 2025: Home Assistant
item.description:
Unauthenticated RCE chain on Home Assistant Green at Pwn2Own Cork 2025 escalates from a Music Assistant add-on to full host root, earning Compass Security $20,000 and 4 Master of Pwn points.
Three bugs chained: no auth on port 8095, arbitrary file write via playlist path manipulation, and plaintext token sniffing across containers running on a shared host network.
- Music Assistant 2.6.0 exposed its web interface on port 8095 without authentication, a deliberate workaround for OAuth callback issues merged months before the competition. Any LAN host could reach the full API without credentials. The attacker created a local filesystem provider rooted at /, then used the music/playlists/update command to reassign a playlist's storage path to an arbitrary location, bypassing the .m3u extension enforcement. Adding a track to that playlist triggered a write to the chosen path, with partial content control via the uris field. By injecting a newline into the uris value, the team wrote an "import os; os.system(...)" line into /app/venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/csnc.pth, a Python .pth file. The Python site[.]py interpreter executes import-prefixed lines in .pth files at process startup, turning the file write into code execution.
- The .pth payload fired when the ytmusic provider was initialized via config/providers/save. That provider's handle_async_init calls _install_packages, which invokes uv pip install through asyncio.create_subprocess_exec, spawning a fresh Python process that loads site-packages and triggers the reverse shell. The resulting shell ran as root inside the Music Assistant container, because the add-on process itself runs as root within its Docker environment.
- Container escape relied on two misconfigurations in the Music Assistant config.yaml: host_network: true and homeassistant_api: true. Because the container shared the host network namespace, tcpdump on the internal interface captured plaintext HTTP between containers and the Supervisor at 172.30.32.2:80. Within roughly 5 minutes, a scheduled Home Assistant Core request to /os/info passed a full bearer token in an Authorization header. That token carried hassio_api privileges the Music Assistant token lacked.
- With the stolen Core token, the attacker registered a malicious GitHub-hosted add-on repository via POST /store/repositories, installed the add-on via POST /addons/4b60877e_compass-ssh-container/install, silently disabled protection mode via POST /addons/4b60877e_compass-ssh-container/security with {"protected":false} bypassing the UI warning dialog entirely, and started the add-on. The privileged add-on exposed SSH on port 8000. From there, docker run --privileged -v /:/host with all capabilities, no AppArmor, no seccomp, and all host namespaces shared gave a shell mapping container root to host root. A chroot /host completed the full host takeover.
Affected versions: Music Assistant add-on 2.6.0, Core 2025.10.3, Supervisor 2025.10.0, OS 16.2, Frontend 20251001.2. Music Assistant 2.7.0 adds authentication to port 8095 and rejects item_id changes for filesystem-based playlist providers.
Practitioner takeaway: for anyone defending Home Assistant deployments, the artifact trail here spans container network captures, Supervisor API logs showing unexpected repository registration and add-on installs, and new .pth files in Python site-packages directories. Hunt for add-on protection mode changes made via API rather than the UI, unexpected docker run --privileged invocations in host process logs, and any outbound connections from add-on containers to attacker infrastructure. Verify no add-on carries host_network: true unless strictly required, and audit which containers are granted hassio_api or homeassistant_api flags. The Supervisor's internal HTTP bus carries privileged tokens in plaintext: shared host networking is a container escape waiting for a listener.

item.title: Symantec reports Warlock ransomware group targets water, telecom, government organizations through SharePoint flaws
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 Longlegs group hits water, telecom, and government targets across Europe, Africa, and Latin America with Warlock ransomware, exploiting on-premises SharePoint Server flaws more than a year after initial disclosure.
Key details:
- The ToolShell vulnerability chain, CVE-2025-49704, CVE-2025-49706, CVE-2025-53770, and CVE-2025-53771, gave Longlegs (also tracked as Storm-2603) its original foothold in June 2025. Symantec's report indicates newer SharePoint flaws flagged by CISA in a July 2026 advisory are now also in play, meaning unpatched on-premises SharePoint remains open ground for this group.
- The webshell landing zone is the SharePoint LAYOUTS directory. Longlegs drops it to cover multiple SharePoint versions simultaneously, then harvests the farm's ASP.NET machine keys. Those keys let the attackers forge a validly signed payload that achieves remote code execution inside the SharePoint application pool, a technique that bypasses signature-based detection because the payload appears legitimately signed.
- SYSVOL is the ransomware delivery mechanism. By staging Warlock inside the compromised domain's SYSVOL share, normal Active Directory replication carries the payload to every domain controller and any domain-joined machine that reads it, allowing deployment across at least 33 hosts in one intrusion without touching each machine individually. Security software was disabled on at least 40 hosts first, accomplished within roughly two hours.
- Longlegs blends into administrative traffic using living-off-the-land tooling and Visual Studio Code's built-in tunnel feature. The group installs code-insiders.exe as a service to maintain covert remote access, a channel that looks like routine developer or administrator activity and can be missed by network monitoring tuned to flag exotic tooling.
- Four organizations were hit over two months: a water utility, a telecommunications provider, a regional government body, and a university, all operating in Portuguese- or Spanish-speaking countries. The inclusion of a water utility underscores the real-world consequence risk when ransomware reaches OT-adjacent environments.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt for webshells in the SharePoint LAYOUTS directory and audit ASP.NET machine key access and recent changes in SharePoint farm configuration. On the AD side, check SYSVOL for executables or staged payloads that have no business being there, and review replication logs for unusual file distribution. Look for code-insiders.exe running as a service, especially outside developer workstations. If your environment runs on-premises SharePoint and has not applied the ToolShell patches plus the fixes referenced in the July 2026 CISA advisory, treat exposure as active. The full IOC list is in Symantec's report.

item.title: UAT-11587 Antino Backdoor Campaign Targeting Government and Policy Organizations Across Asia
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 nexus actor UAT-11587 hit 16+ government and policy orgs across Asia with Antino, a Rust-compiled backdoor that hides its C2 inside Microsoft 365 traffic.
Key details:
- Antino is a previously undocumented Rust-compiled Windows backdoor with host recon, PowerShell and command execution, file transfer, in-memory shellcode loading, and persistence. Its C2 runs entirely over Microsoft Graph, Outlook, and OneDrive, meaning malicious traffic terminates at graph[.]microsoft[.]com and login.microsoftonline[.]com, legitimate endpoints that IP/domain blocklists will not catch. Network-only detection will miss this campaign.
- The infection chain runs: spear-phishing lure with government or maritime themes, malicious link or attachment, HTA/WSF stager, JavaScript downloader, .NET deserialization, then Antino dropped as slc.dll. Payload staging used Cloudflare Pages, Cloudflare R2, and Amazon CloudFront, all legitimate services. Watch for mshta.exe, WScript, and CScript spawning from email clients or user-writable paths.
- Persistence and delivery rely on DLL sideloading: a legitimate Microsoft-signed GatherOsState.exe loads the malicious slc.dll. A signed parent binary will not trigger signature-based alerts alone. Hunt for GatherOsState.exe executing outside its expected path and check loaded DLLs for slc.dll in unusual locations.
- The Philippines 🇵🇭 was specifically targeted from September 2025, with a lure titled "Resolution on the Updated Chart of Bajo de Masinloc" aimed at the Philippine 🇵🇭 public sector. Taiwan 🇹🇼, India 🇮🇳, Cambodia 🇰🇭, Pakistan 🇵🇰, Thailand 🇹🇭, Myanmar 🇲🇲, and Syria were also targeted. At least 350 compromised endpoints were identified by July 2026 across 16 institutional environments spanning government, defense, diplomatic, legislative, law enforcement, and civil society sectors.
- The Microsoft 365 C2 channel means the full detection picture requires combining endpoint telemetry with Entra ID, OAuth application logs, and Microsoft 365 audit logs. Look for OAuth apps with Graph Mail or Files read/write permissions that were recently consented to by a user, unexpected Outlook or OneDrive API calls from non-standard processes, and unusual authentication patterns in Entra ID sign-in logs alongside suspicious DLL loads or PowerShell activity on the same endpoint timeline.
Takeaway: Hunt across EDR, SIEM, and Microsoft 365 audit logs simultaneously. GatherOsState.exe loading slc.dll is a concrete endpoint artifact to search for now. Check OAuth app consent events in Entra ID for unexpected Graph permissions granted around the campaign window (September 2025 to July 2026). The Cisco Talos report contains the full IOC list including hashes, domains, and URLs.

item.title: Anatomía de BraZetsu: Cómo los cibercriminales abastecen el ecosistema clandestino
item.description:
BraZetsu: a Brazilian 🇧🇷 Python-based IAB framework attributed to threat actor Exilware targets Iberian and Latin American corporate, financial, industrial, and law enforcement environments, feeding a commercial access marketplace since February 2026.
Key findings:
- BraZetsu is a modular, Python 3 framework compiled with Nuitka into standalone PE executables, a choice that defeats signature-based detection and complicates reverse engineering. At time of analysis, the latest v5 build was fully undetectable on VirusTotal. The framework retrieves its C2 config as a Base64, XOR-encrypted blob from Pastebin dead-drop resolvers (e.g., hxxps://pastebin[.]com/raw/aF0WCxia), decoded with the hardcoded key p4st3_s3cr3t_k3y, then parses the c2_domain, port, and auth_token from a pipe-delimited string. All C2 traffic runs over a persistent WebSocket connection on TLS port 8443, pointed at c2.installscenter[.]com and the VPS at 38.242.246[.]176.
- The framework's get_stealth_iab_tags function profiles every compromised host across roughly 20 categories: FINANCE_ERP (SAP, TOTVS/Protheus, Warsaw, Topaz, Diebold), SCADA_INDUSTRIAL (FactoryTalk, RSLogix, WinCC), BACKUP_SERVER (veeam.exe, bengine.exe), SECURITY_EDR (csfalconservice.exe for CrowdStrike, sentinelagent.exe for SentinelOne, msmpeng.exe for Defender), LAW_ENFORCEMENT (hostname prefixes PC-, PM-, DP-, SSP-), HEALTHCARE_HIS (Tasy ERP, DICOM port 104), and DEVOPS_CLOUD (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AZURE_CONFIG_DIR, KUBECONFIG). Profiled hosts are priced and listed on Infected Marketplace at infect[.]online and infectonline[.]store with a minimum deposit of roughly USD 5.80.
- Rather than stealing credentials or cookies, BraZetsu's get_browser_intel function copies Chrome, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi, and Opera SQLite History databases to %TEMP% using shutil.copyfile to bypass file locks, then runs the query SELECT url, title, visit_count FROM urls WHERE url LIKE ? against a TARGET_DOMAINS list of approximately 230 domains spanning banking, ERP, e-commerce, and government portals. The function ler_e_preparar_certificados recursively hunts the user profile and OneDrive for .pfx and .p12 digital certificates and exfiltrates them bundled in a dossier. The function obter_identidade_v8 uses regex to extract CPF and CNPJ legal identifiers. File extensions actively hunted include .cnab, .240, .400, .rem, and .ret.
- Log strings embedded in the code reference a server-side AI engine: "Coleta metadados de hardware e porte da máquina para a IA do servidor" and "Define se o arquivo é um alvo prioritário para a IA." The volume of emoji-annotated Portuguese 🇵🇹 logging ([], [], []) is consistent with LLM-assisted development. The framework tracks as AgenteV2 in prior ANY.RUN reporting, sharing loader names wifi_driver.exe and msedge04.exe, payload temp_agente.dll (equivalent to agenteV2_historico_detect.dll), identical Python 3.13 plus Nuitka build environments, and the same 38.242.246[.]176 VPS. Persistence in v1 was established via a Run key named MonitorSystem under SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run.
- Initial distribution runs through the domain caixaentradas1inboxshop[.]site using VBS droppers masquerading as a judicial notification ("processo de intimação") and file patterns msdege[0-9].exe and wifi_driver.exe. The same infrastructure distributed the Ousaban banking trojan. Buyers on Infected Marketplace can remotely execute their own payloads against purchased accesses via the _execute_worker function, creating a persistent threat-multiplication effect. Two US 🇺🇸 compromised hosts appeared for sale in April 2026, a potential indicator of geographic expansion.
Hunt priority: search endpoints running TOTVS, SAP, Senior, or Tasy for processes spawning cmd.exe (T1059.003) with WebSocket connections to external IPs on port 8443, and audit %TEMP% for copies of Chrome and Edge History SQLite databases alongside a file named debug_payload_sent.json. Flag outbound connections to Pastebin from hosts running ERP or SCADA software. Full IOC list including 16 file hashes, C2 domains, and Pastebin resolver URLs is in the Group-IB report. MITRE ATT&CK coverage spans T1012, T1083, T1217, T1113, T1027.002, and T1564.003 among others.

item.title: GlassWorm Goes Mac: Fresh Infrastructure, New Tricks
item.description:
GlassWorm's fourth wave pivots to macOS, planting three malicious Open VSX extensions with roughly 50,000 reported downloads and adding Ledger Live and Trezor Suite replacement logic to its existing credential-theft playbook.
Key findings:
- The three extensions (studio-velte-distributor.pro-svelte-extension, cudra-production.vsce-prettier-pro, Puccin-development.full-access-catppuccin-pro-extension) embedded AES-256-CBC-encrypted payloads using a hardcoded key shared across all three samples. A 15-minute timer (9e5 ms) delayed execution, a sandbox-evasion attempt that fails against combined static and dynamic analysis since the encrypted blob, key, IV, and timer are all visible in the JavaScript before it ever runs.
- The macOS payload establishes LaunchAgent persistence, uses AppleScript to invoke shell commands and query the Keychain via the security utility, and copies ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db to a local staging directory at /tmp/ijewf/ before compressing and exfiltrating to 45.32.150[.]251/p2p. Collection scope is broad: 50-plus browser wallet extensions, desktop wallets including Electrum and Atomic, GitHub tokens from VS Code storage, npm tokens from .npmrc, SSH keys from ~/.ssh, VPN configs, and browser cookies across Chrome, Firefox, Brave, and Edge.
- C2 discovery runs through the Solana blockchain. The malware queries address BjVeAjPrSKFiingBn4vZvghsGj9KCE8AJVtbc9S8o8SC, decodes base64-encoded URLs from transaction memos, and contacts the referenced server. A November 27, 2025 transaction pointed to 217.69.11[.]60; by December the active C2 was 45.32.151[.]157, an IP also seen in Wave 3. Blocking a domain does not touch a discovery mechanism recorded on a public blockchain.
- Wallet replacement logic checked for Ledger Live and Trezor Suite application directories via AppleScript, then attempted to download a trojanized replacement, remove the legitimate app, and install the attacker copy. During December 29 testing the replacement endpoints returned empty files and the routine rejected downloads under 1,000 bytes, so successful trojanization was not confirmed. The credential-collection and persistence paths were operational at the time of investigation.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt your macOS developer endpoints for LaunchAgent entries created by an editor process, unexpected invocations of the security utility targeting Keychain items, file writes to /tmp/ijewf/, and outbound connections to 45.32.151[.]157 or 45.32.150[.]251. Where the payload executed, treat it as a full incident: isolate the host, preserve LaunchAgent plists and the staged archive before remediation, then rotate every credential the machine could reach (GitHub tokens, npm tokens, SSH keys) from a clean system and audit associated repository and package-publishing activity. The IOC table and extension identifiers are in the report.
